#3497. Robert Pattinson's James Bond Casting Breaks A 60-Year-Old 007 Tradition

It's official: We have our new 007. Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond and will take over for Daniel Craig, whose run concluded in 2021 with "No Time to Die." Now, a full five years later, Amazon and MGM have finally firmed up who will be filling in the legendary character's shoes for his latest cinematic chapter. And while Pattinson is undoubtedly an actor with a lot of experience, his casting does break a tradition that has been going for more than 60 years.

1962's "Dr. No" kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise with "James Bond," based on Ian Fleming's series of novels. Sean Connery famously played 007 in that movie, with his run expanding through 1971's "Diamonds are Forever." He did return to the part once more for "Never Say Never Again," but that's not technically an official entry in the "Bond" movie canon. In any case, it's the role that went on to define Connery's career, as it generally has for every other actor who's picked up the baton after him.

Becoming James Bond was a double-edged sword for Connery, as it was at times hard for people to see him as anything other than the famed MI6 spy. But that was sort of by design. What the producers of the "Bond" franchise generally did was cast an actor who had experience but wasn't necessarily an A-list movie star. That allowed them to truly become Bond, not just on screen but in the eyes of the viewing public. That's where Pattinson truly differs.

Pattinson broke out as Edward Cullen in the "Twilight" films before starring in a string of acclaimed indies. More recently, he played Bruce Wayne in "The Batman." That matters a lot.

Robert Pattinson isn't just a big movie star, he's one who has a handful of beloved characters under his belt. A lot of people will always associate him with "Twilight." That's why it was hard for certain folks to see him as Batman until "The Batman" came out. People are now going to see him as the Caped Crusader for years to come, especially with "The Batman Part II" in the works.

Amazon currently controls the "James Bond" films, though, and it's willing to buck tradition. Amazon's Jeff Bezos reached his breaking point with the franchise's original producers, Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, ultimately buying them out. Had Broccoli and Wilson been involved, it's less likely that an actor with as much cache as Pattinson would have won out against the likes of Callum Turner ("Eternity") and Josh O'Connor ("Challengers"), who were among the finalists.

On paper, Pattinson does fit the bill in every other way. James Bond is never young, and Pattinson is 40. That's almost the exact same age that Pierce Brosnan was when he took over for "GoldenEye." Roger Moore was 45 when he took over in "Live and Let Die." Even Daniel Craig was 38 in "Casino Royale," which was an origin story for him as 007. He's meant to be a seasoned veteran. He's not a rookie. But Moore ("The Saint") and Brosnan ("Remington Steele") were more TV stars than movie stars.

There's no denying that Pattinson has the look. We've seen him shine in suits in movies like "Tenet" and "Cosmopolis." He's also turned into one heck of an actor and is currently in the mix to win Best Actor at next year's Oscars for his role in "Primetime."

It also doesn't hurt that the actor previously worked with director Denis Villeneuve on "Dune: Part Three," which hits theaters in December. After that, Villeneuve is heading right into production on the currently untitled "James Bond 26." There's a rapport there between the two. It's easy to see the appeal of Robert Pattinson as 007, particularly for Amazon.

Much has changed in Hollywood in the 20 years since Daniel Craig took over for Pierce Brosnan in "Casino Royale." James Bond isn't the slam dunk movie star he once was, so to speak, and Amazon needs this franchise to work for a new generation. Casting a bankable star like Pattinson, whom audiences very much like, adds some insurance. Case in point, Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" (which co-stars Pattinson) has ruled the box office with more than $1.8 billion to its name this year. So, Pattinson has a great track record even outside of big franchises.

Naturally, fans are going to feel big feelings about Pattinson as Bond. Craig has no hard feelings about his "Casino Royale" casting controversy, but it's worth remembering that people flipped out when he was announced. Now? He's perhaps the most beloved actor in the franchise's history. The actor has to prove himself once he's cast, regardless of what fans think. That's always been the case.

Pattinson absolutely has to shoulder that same responsibility now. The question is, can people see him as James Bond more than Edward Cullen or Batman? Can he assert himself as Bond so definitively that his history doesn't overshadow what's on screen? That's some extra baggage that his predecessors didn't necessarily have to carry.

The new "James Bond" movie doesn't have a release date yet, but stay tuned.

#3496. The Acer Predator Atlas 7 is my favorite handheld of 2026 and it cures the memory pricing crisis in style

The Acer Predator Atlas 7 sticks a middle finger up to RAMageddon and strikes the right balance of price, raw performance and efficient software — overcoming a few ergonomic quirks and a smaller battery to become my favorite handheld of 2026.

Significantly cheaper than Z2 Extreme competition

Included matte screen protector fixes glossy display reflections

Display’s not the brightest or most colorful

Dual-fan cooling system gets loud under load

Shallow grips have never been my cup of tea

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Handheld gaming has become one of the most exciting, yet terrifying, categories in tech. It feels great to have your PC library with you everywhere, but to get there, you either grab something that’s underpowered and overpriced, or you skip rent for a month to get something actually good.

The Acer Predator Atlas 7 is the rare exception to that rule.

At £900 in the U.K. (not available in the U.S. in this base configuration yet), it is a rather unassuming slab of a handheld that hides a monster inside: an Intel Arc G3 chip paired with 16GB of LPDDR5X memory.

It easily outmuscles more expensive AMD Ryzen Z2 Extreme competitors while dodging massive component price hikes. And while you will have to manage that smaller 60Wh battery and some loud fans, the sheer gaming grunt for that price makes it my undeniable handheld of the year.

7-inch HD (1920 x 1080) LCD 120Hz refresh rate

1x Micro SD, 2x Thunderbolt 4, 1x 3.5mm audio jack

So as I started taking this on solo trips to the pub (yep, I’m that guy) and on my travels all over the place, I started to really see the strengths in the Atlas 7.

The real superpower is what’s inside: the highly efficient Intel Arc G3 equipped with a B370 GPU and 16GB of LPDDR5X memory. Up until this point, I’d only tested the Arc G3 Extreme, so I was a little nervous heading into its smaller, weaker sibling.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 (AMD Ryzen Z2 AI Extreme)

The Arc G3 gives you enough breathing room to push your 1080p settings, and sits comfortably above the capabilities of the Ryzen Z2 Extreme in the ROG Xbox Ally X20 — a handheld that’s a third more expensive.

Plus, when you slap Intel’s XeSS and multi-frame generation on top of a solid baseline frame rate, it feels properly zippy and responsive.

On a compact 7-inch screen, you don’t see the ghosting or sizzling artifacts that you would on a bigger desktop monitor with the Arc B580 GPU.

Asus ROG Xbox Ally X (AMD Ryzen Z2 AI Extreme)

There is an anomaly in the Black Myth: Wukong benchmark, but for every other game it was all Intel domination. I think that may be down to optimization for particular silicon.

On top of that, it is also an extremely capable docked system; Star Wars Galactic Racer ran incredibly smooth at 1440p on medium settings with XeSS set to Performance mode.

And don’t get me wrong. You’ll get much more from the Extreme variant, but you’re paying much more to take it up a notch. With the Arc, this much power at this price is right on the money.

Acer nailed the inputs here. They opted for TMR joysticks, which are incredibly smooth and highly reliable since there are no internal gears grinding away. The face buttons offer a satisfying, tactile clickiness, and while the triggers have a decent amount of depth, I do wish they had a slightly more defined flick to catch my fingers.

That being said though, this is a nice lightweight system that sees its mass evenly distributed for level playing.

Windows 11 has finally improved significantly for handhelds. This has been the result of months of work sharpening up the setup process — no more nagging screens asking if you want an Office 365 subscription, just a quick login, some updates and you are ready to play.

For hardware tweaking, that’s where Acer’s PredatorSense overlay comes in. Pressing the top left button triggers it, and while I’d say Asus’ ROG overlay has a slightly nicer UI, PredatorSense puts all the essential customization settings right within a thumb’s reach without overcomplicating things.

But to get something together as a value for money proposition, you have to make some compromises.

The most obvious one is the battery. It’s still sort of decent longevity wise, especially if you get into dropping the TDP to its lowest possible setting and cranking out some indie games. But in our lab test, it’s not great.

This surprised me given the effectiveness of those efficiency cores on the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ and its Arc G3 Extreme. But no amount of efficient silicon can overcome a smaller cell.

Out of the box, the Atlas 7 shares similar ergonomics with the old ROG Ally and Steam Deck, featuring shallower grips that aren’t as ergonomically sound as the chunkier grips on the Ally X20. The end result is a system you’d lean on a table more than comfortably suspended in the air.

Thermally, the dual-fan cooling system delivers impressive sustained performance, keeping the back of the device nice and cool even at peak output. But the trade-off is noise; those fans do get loud when the system is fully unleashed.

And finally, the 120Hz display has color and is visible indoors, but the brightness isn’t quite there for playing by a window/strong light source. Plus the glossy finish turns that screen into a mirror, though Acer thankfully includes a matte screen protector in the box.

The Acer Predator Atlas 7 leaves me conflicted, but in the best way possible.

For all intents and purposes, this is the best handheld of the year. Yes, there are devices with better displays, chunkier ergonomics and better battery life. But in terms of striking a strong enough mix across all metrics, Acer’s nailed it.

At £900, it is significantly cheaper than the competition it beats, but I also admit that it's hard to call almost a grand “cheap.” That being said, in the midst of a component crisis where competing devices approach the £2,000 mark with worse performance, the Atlas 7 actually makes you feel like you’re getting your money’s worth.

#3495. No, We Aren’t All Eating 'Too Much' Protein

If you’ll permit me a rant—I promise to make it fact-filled and interesting—I am sick of the articles that seem to pop up every few months claiming that we are all eating “too much” protein. They convey an inaccurate picture of how the body uses protein, and they demonize perfectly healthy meals that happen to be high in protein. It’s time to set the record straight.

It is true that most of us eat more than the RDA (recommended daily allowance) of protein, but that's a good thing—the RDA is meant as a minimum. It's true that protein-boosted foods are trendy, and that they're not necessarily great dietary choices in the big picture. It's also true that you can eat a healthy diet with little to no meat, but meat is not synonymous with protein. Let's look at what we actually know about the role of protein in a healthy diet, and how to tell if you're eating too much or too little.

As a refresher, protein is one of the three calorie-containing macronutrients (fats, carbs, protein) that make up most of the food we eat. Proteins are made of amino acids, and these amino acids are required for the growth, repair, and functioning of our bodies.

We can get protein from a variety of sources. Meats are particularly protein-dense; a chicken breast contains about 35 grams of protein. Other animal products, like milk and eggs, are also rich in protein. Plant-based foods tend to have less protein than animal products, but it’s not hard to meet or exceed protein requirements even on a vegan diet. Beans, grains, and soy products like tofu contain significant amounts of protein, for example.

If you’d like a cheat sheet on how much protein you’re supposed to eat based on your activity level, you can find one here. And that’s a good place to start dissecting this “too much protein” myth, because before we can declare an amount of protein to be “too much,” we need to understand how much is “enough.”

The government communicates targets for different nutrients to encourage us all to eat a healthy, balanced diet. These targets are the basis for the “% daily value” labels on the back of packaged foods, and for the nutrient makeup of school lunches. The RDA, or recommended daily allowance, is defined as “the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all (97 to 98 percent) healthy individuals in a group.”

In other words, if 100% of us were to eat the RDA of protein, at least 97% of us would be getting enough protein—we'd be meeting the minimum to be healthy. That's right, this number is a minimum to avoid malnutrition, not a maximum, and not a recommendation for optimal health.

By the way, if you're wondering how that number is determined? For protein, it is based on nitrogen balance. Humans break down proteins, as part of our body’s daily function, and we excrete nitrogen as a result. If you eat enough protein (which contains nitrogen), the amount of nitrogen you excrete will be the same as, or more than, the amount you eat. In other words, if you aren’t breaking your own body proteins down (in excess of what you eat), then whatever you’re eating must be, in some sense, enough.

In this way of thinking, the RDA is the minimum to stay healthy. More is fine; less would mean that you may not be getting enough. For some nutrients, there is also an UL, or upper limit, telling you that more than a certain amount is too much. Upper limits are calculated for vitamins and minerals; there is no upper limit defined for protein.

Therefore, there is no official definition for “too much” protein. If somebody eats more than the RDA, they’re not eating too much; they’re just eating more than the minimum. You’re supposed to eat more than the minimum.

The RDA for protein is set at 46 grams per day for a 125-pound woman, and at 56 grams per day for a 154-pound man. (The USDA chose those as their examples.) That’s based on an RDA of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram bodyweight, which works out to 0.36 grams per pound. So a 200-pound person would need 72 grams of protein per day.

This USDA report found that most adult men average roughly 90 to 100 grams of protein per day, although men aged 70 and up only get about 80 grams of protein per day. Women tend to average around 70 grams per day, with those aged 70 and up averaging 62 grams.

Above the RDA? Yes. Too much? I don’t see any way of arguing that. And before you say that we’re getting almost double the recommendation, let's check the math. Those RDA numbers are for 125- and 154-pound people. On the other hand, the averages for what we eat are based on actual people, not ideals. The average American man is 200 pounds, and the average American woman is 171 pounds. So, to compare the numbers:

The average woman is 171 pounds, so her RDA would be 62 grams per day. (Women, on average, eat 70 grams of protein per day.)

The average man is 200 pounds, so his RDA would be 72 grams per day. (Men, on average, eat 90 to 100 grams of protein per day.)

Again, there’s no need to stick to the minimum; going 8 grams over, or even 28 grams over, is fine. It’s probably better to go over than to just scrape by, and many of us arguably don’t get enough. Let me explain.

Let’s start with older adults. Not only does protein intake tend to decrease with age, older adults are vulnerable to issues that stem from a loss of muscle mass. People tend to lose 3-5% of their muscle mass per decade starting at age 30, but strength training and protein intake can support maintaining our muscle, and thus likely prevent or reduce that decline.

The Dietary Guidelines include a note that “About 50 percent of women and 30 percent of men 71 and older fall short of protein foods recommendations.” Meanwhile, a study found that older adults who don’t meet the recommendations are “more likely to be limited when stooping, crouching, or kneeling, standing or sitting for long periods, walking up 10 steps, preparing meals, and walking for a quarter mile.”

So even if it’s true that the average adult gets more protein than recommended, there are clearly a lot of elderly folks who don’t. These are the same people who have more issues functioning in everyday life. This may be a chicken-and-egg situation—was the functional decline a cause or an effect of the change in their diet?—but this sure does not seem to be a group of people who should be eating less protein.

There’s another large group of people who benefit from more, not less, protein: people who are pregnant or lactating. Instead of 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight (62 grams for a 171-pound person), the RDA for people who are pregnant or lactating is 0.5 grams/pound (so, 86 grams of protein per day).

When you’re pregnant, you also have higher caloric needs, so the increased total amount of food makes it easier to get the higher protein amount. Still, it makes more sense to spend your energy on making sure you’re getting enough protein, rather than worrying about getting too much.

You knew we were heading in this direction (I say between reps of barbell squats, wiping protein shake off my lips): People who exercise should get more protein than just the RDA.

While the fear-mongering “too much protein” articles sometimes mention that bodybuilders or elite athletes need their protein, they tend to hand-wave this away as a special concern that doesn’t apply to normal people. But I think it’s worth a closer look—and honestly, this situation applies to a lot more people than just a few athletes.

Officially, there isn’t an RDA for athletes; people who exercise can stave off malnutrition with the same 0.36 grams per pound as everyone else. But that doesn’t mean that the RDA is the best target to aim for.

The International Association of Athletics Federations, which governs track and field competitions, recommends that most athletes who are maintaining or gaining weight eat 0.59 to 0.77 grams of protein per pound of bodyweight per day. That’s 101 to 131 grams for the average 171-pound woman, and 118 to 154 grams for a 200-pound man.

A group of organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, largely agrees, recommending a range from 0.54 to 0.9 grams per pound for all athletes whose weight is stable or gaining. That includes people who do endurance training like distance running, as well as strength athletes whose exercise involves mainly lifting weights. Those ranges would go as high as 153 grams for our 171-pound woman, and 180 grams for our 200-pound man.

You don’t need to be an Olympian to consider yourself an “athlete” in this sense. If you’re training for a half marathon, you’re doing plenty of distance running, and should fuel accordingly. And if you’re “just” lifting weights in the gym, but taking it seriously enough that you’re training regularly and working hard, you should consider eating in these ranges as well.

Dieting to lose weight is not only a popular American pastime, it’s also arguably good for at least some people's health. If you’ve been on a diet recently, or if you’re planning to go on one, you aren’t a person who should settle for the RDA either.

Research shows that protein intake (and strength training—they go together!) is important to maintain muscle mass when we’re losing weight. After all, you’re aiming for fat loss, not trying to get your muscles to waste away. Muscle loss is especially a concern with weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, but any dieter should be aware of this issue.

For example, this study found that diets ranging from 0.48 to 0.72 grams of protein per kg of body weight (that’s 82 to 123 grams for our 171-pound woman, 96 to 144 for our 200-pound man) resulted in less weight regain after the diet, and helped people to maintain muscle mass and feel more full while they were dieting.

And if you’re losing weight and exercising? The IAAF recommends that athletes who are “undertaking high-quality weight loss” need at least 0.72 grams per pound of bodyweight, and possibly as much as 1.09 grams per pound. That would be 186 grams for a 171-pound athlete, or 218 grams for a 200-pound athlete. Most people won’t need to go that high, and it’s unclear whether athletes need to go that high. But I’m including these numbers so you see how high the ranges actually go.

Ultimately, weight loss is widely understood to be more effective and have healthier results with higher protein intakes rather than lower ones. When people focus on just eating less, without thinking about what their diet actually consists of, it’s easy to forget about protein. But the evidence suggests that you should increase protein when you’re decreasing overall calories.

The idea that protein causes weight gain is a common talking point in those articles about “too much” protein, and it’s sort of true—but it also doesn’t mean what you think it means.

When you eat more food than your body needs, your body can store it as fat. That’s true no matter what the excess is made of—protein, carbs, fat, or even alcohol. The protein you eat gets used for many different things in your body. You can build it into muscle tissue, use it for growth and repair of different kinds of cells, and so on. You can also use it for energy—basically, burning it for the calories.

So if you were eating a perfectly balanced diet, and then decided to add an extra 100 grams of protein per day, then sure, a lot of that protein would be used for energy, and since we’d have excess energy, it would get stored as fat.

But if you ate more protein, but that protein replaced other foods in your diet, then there would be no excess calories to store. Nobody is saying you should chug a couple of protein shakes on top of your regular diet. They’re saying (I’m saying) that you should plan your meals and snacks to include more protein.

For example, if your regular lunch is a turkey-and-cheese sandwich with a side of chips, you could improve the protein content of your diet by adding more turkey to the sandwich and replacing the chips with an apple. Same total calories, but more protein. As long as your total calories for the day aren’t in excess of your needs, the “extra” protein won’t get stored as fat.

In general, high protein diets don’t have any serious health consequences. There’s a major exception, though: in some medical conditions, you may be told to limit your protein intake to protect your health.

For example, people with chronic kidney disease are often advised to use the RDA (0.36 grams per pound of body weight) as a maximum rather than a minimum. Your kidneys play a role in processing protein for excretion, so a lowered protein intake reduces the amount of work that a damaged kidney has to do. That said, once a person with chronic kidney disease begins dialysis, they may be advised to increase their protein intake for better health now that their body has help to handle the higher levels.

People with certain other disorders, like phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, may also be advised to eat a low-protein diet. Obviously, if you have one of these conditions, you should be getting your dietary advice from your medical team (ask for a referral to a dietitian!) rather than from general articles on the internet.

Besides those known medical issues, the occasional findings about eating “too much” protein tend to fit into the “X is good for you/X is bad for you” ricochet news cycle. They’re not holistic assessments of protein in general on health in general, but rather specific research questions that are still being figured out.

For example, this 2017 study found that a high-protein (and high-fiber) diet seemed to slightly worsen one measure of insulin resistance, but it also improved metabolic health and body composition. The researchers concluded that the subjects’ body chemistry was probably just responding appropriately to the changed nutrient content of their diet. A few years later, a study of high-BMI women with insulin resistance saw improvements to their insulin resistance on a high-protein diet.

Or to take another example, a study in 2024 found a link between high-protein diets and atherosclerosis. But if you look at what the researchers were actually studying, they were looking at how leucine (one amino acid found in protein) affects the mTOR biochemical pathway in certain types of white blood cells. By the way, that mTOR pathway is involved in a lot more body processes than atherosclerosis, and does a lot of good things too.

So are these results interesting, and worth further study? Definitely. Worth changing protein recommendations? Only if this effect turns out (1) to actually lead to worse health outcomes, and (2) to outweigh the known benefits of higher protein. The body of evidence doesn’t yet support lowering protein recommendations, nor adding an upper limit.

So if protein is good for us, and most of us can’t really get “too much,” why are so many people arguing that we’re overdoing it? I think part of the reason is just misunderstanding (the writers don’t tend to have a background in nutrition and especially not in sports nutrition), but more often, I think they’re talking about a different issue entirely.

Often the “too much protein” stuff is just a way of talking about the environmental effects of meat consumption or dairy farming. People making this argument are trying to pry the double cheeseburgers out of our hands and reassure us that we’ll be okay. I don’t think an attack on protein is an appropriate way to make that point, since plant-based proteins exist and are a fine alternative. But I understand where they’re coming from.

Ultimately, if you’re trying to make the argument that we’re eating “too much” protein for our health, you really can’t do that without some evidence that we’re eating so much protein that it’s harming our health on a widespread level. And that evidence just doesn’t exist.

#3494. Jennifer Lawrence Dropped A Throwback Post With The Hunger Games’ Peeta And Gale (And Her Caption Is A+)

It’s hard to believe it’s been over 14 years since audiences first saw Jennifer Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen volunteer as tribute for the 74th Hunger Games. While so much time has passed, that series of book-to-screen adaptations remains greatly loved by fans. Lawrence herself seems to have an appreciation for that time in her life as well even if it wasn’t always easy for her to control the craziness. Ahead of her return as Katniss, Lawrence shared a sweet throwback pic of herself with two of her key co-stars, and her caption is great.

Lawrence is set to play Katniss for the first time in over a decade in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, which is set to hit the 2026 movie schedule in a matter of days. It would seem that the Oscar winner is feeling a bit nostalgic, as she recently took to her Instagram stories to share some classic pics, possibly from press tours from the early aughts. One particularly sweet photo shows Lawrence alongside Peeta Mellark actor Josh Hutcherson and Gale Hawthorne star Liam Hemsworth. Check out it below:

The mere sight of this lovely photo is enough to hit someone with a hearty helping of early 2010s nostalgia. I can still remember the sheer amount of buzz that surrounded the release of the first Hunger Games movie adapted from Suzanne Collins’ beloved book series. What we see in that picture are the smiling faces of three people in the midst of an amazing professional journey. Also, leave it to “J. Law” to choose such a cheeky caption for the photo and, let’s be real, the statement isn’t untrue either.

What I really want to know is when exactly this photo was taken. I mean, was this taken around the time the OG film in the young adult franchise came out or at a later date. Regardless, I appreciate Lawrence sharing such sweet mementos, and you can check out another post down below. This one features two black-and-white photos — one of the trio hanging out on what appears to be a bridge and another shot of them on a bed:

Jennifer Lawrence is practically revered for her role as Katniss at this point, as many still hold her performance in high regard, including others who’ve since joined the franchise. Earlier this year, Sunrise on the Reaping’s Maya Hawke praised Lawrence for her character’s impact on the action genre. Ironically, Lawrence explained years ago that she was scared to sign on for the movies, given such blockbusters can “make or break a career.” I think it’s safe to say that everything turned out fine, though.

Josh Hutcherson has also expressed warm feelings about the reception he’s received for his performance as Peeta, which has blown fans away. Though Hutcherson had been away from the franchise for some time, he admitted last fall that he felt a bit of FOMO over not being a part of the newer films. That has changed, however, as Hutcherson is reprising Peeta alongside Lawrence’s Katniss and Woody Harrelson’s (older) Haymitch Abernathy in the latest installment.

How exactly that aforementioned trio of actors factors into this prequel film is unclear at the moment. Nevertheless, I’m sure fans are just pleased that they’ll be returning in some kind of capacity. For now, though, I just find it lovely that Jennifer Lawrence is embracing her memories, and I hope she and the “girls” are able to somehow make some new ones down the road.

Check out The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping when it opens in theaters on November 20. In the meantime, stream the original four films now with a Peacock subscription, or check them out for free on Tubi.

#3493. Anne Hathaway's 2026 Sci-Fi Survival Movie Is Officially HBO Max's Biggest Streaming Hit

If you were disappointed by Anne Hathaway's dead-on-arrival Colleen Hoover movie "Verity," you might be interested in streaming one of her 2026 efforts that was actually good. HBO Max users certainly are. After a disappointing box office run, "The End of Oak Street," in which a suburban family is transported to dino-land, is finally getting the attention it deserves on the streamer.

"The End of Oak Street" trailers made it look like the the most fun dinosaur movie in years, and that turned out to be true. But the film is also surprisingly heartfelt, finding time between the dino fights and chase sequences to essentially explore the idea of home — the place where we're all supposed to feel safest — suddenly becoming the most unsafe place you could be. Writer/director David Robert Mitchell certainly delivers spectacle, but it's all in service of the characters and an interesting idea that powers the rest of the film.

Unfortunately, the box office returns for "The End of Oak Street" weren't quite what they could have been. The movie made $121.6 million in theaters on an $85 million budget, and if you know how the box office actually works, you're aware the film almost certainly didn't hit its break even point. Warner Bros. then rushed the movie to digital less than 30 days after it opened theatrically, and it remains unclear just how well it performed. But regardless of whether anyone made any money, the film is well worth a watch. Thankfully, HBO Max users now seem to be giving it the attention it always deserved.

"The End of Oak Street" is a thrilling dinosaur adventure that stars Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor as Denise and Greg Platt. The husband and wife live in a quiet Michigan suburb with their daughter Audrey (Maisy Stella) and son Brian (Christian Convery) circa 1982. Tensions lie beneath the surface of their seemingly idyllic life, though, with Denise feeling unfulfilled, Greg struggling to make ends meet, and the kids feeling like outsiders among their peers. Soon, however, they have bigger problems. One morning, the family wakes up to find their neighborhood has been transported back through time to a prehistoric age. Now, rather than social isolation and looming divorces, the biggest threats they face are of the scaly, sharp-toothed variety.

David Robert Mitchell previously oversaw one of the best horror movies of the 21st Century in "It Follows," but he's since proven he can deliver more traditional big-screen thrills with "The End of Oak Street." And while audiences didn't necessarily show up in droves at the multiplex, the film received positive reviews and earned an 86% "certified fresh" critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. As it were, it appears that HBO Max users are as taken with Mitchell's family drama/dino adventure as most critics.

"The End of Oak Street" hit the streamer on November 13, 2026, and it subsequently shot to number one on the most-watched movies charts in multiple countries, including the United States (per FlixPatrol). At the time of writing, the movie occupies the top spot in 57 countries, and in several cases has been there since its debut. So, if you're yet to watch "The End of Oak Street," take this as a sign to rectify that immediately.

#3492. What Robert Pattinson's James Bond Casting Could Mean For His Batman Future

Is it just me, or is Hollywood shrinking these days? Skydance now owns Warner Bros. Discovery, which comes only a few years removed from Disney swallowing up 20th Century Fox in another corporate merger. Now, the same man has currently laid claim to two of the biggest names in the history of franchise filmmaking. And this is raising all sorts of questions about the fate of one of those names — a certain bat-eared superhero – in the near future.

Yes, today has brought us the martini-shaking news that Robert Pattinson has been officially chosen as our next James Bond. Not only does this mean that Pattinson now has three major IPs under his belt at the same time (including his upcoming role in "Dune: Part Three" later this year), but it also feels like our first major indication of Pattinson's future as Batman. As any Bat-fan can attest to, it hasn't been the easiest journey to bringing "The Batman II" from script to screen. The long-delayed sequel recently hit another setback when director Matt Reeves stepped away from filming, with Steven Soderbergh filling in for him. Making matters worse, the change in leadership for DC Studios following the merger between Warner Bros. Discovery and Skydance-Paramount has further thrown the state of Reeves' standalone films in disarray.

But perhaps this Bond announcement, of all things, could shine some light on Pattinson's role as Batman in the years ahead. Are his days in the cape and cowl numbered? Between some recent reporting and simply reading the tea leaves, we may have an idea of what this means for the future of Pattinson's "The Batman" movies.

Nothing in Hollywood occurs in a vacuum, as Robert Pattinson's James Bond casting throws into sharp relief. After all, who could've predicted the dizzying rise of the guy from "Twilight" becoming one of the industry's most recognizable and bank-breaking leading men of all? As it turns out, that principle also applies to the novelty of seeing the same man cast as both Bond and Batman at the same time — however short-lived that may be.

As fans paying close attention may have guessed, one development likely has much to do with the other. If we look back at the buzzy search for our new Bond over the last several months, it's clear that Pattinson's candidacy (along with Nicholas Hoult's) only cropped up in the eleventh hour. Industry insider Matt Belloni suggested as much in a recent Puck newsletter, handily explaining why most rumors failed to mention Pattinson's name in the early going. What's more, this timing also coincides with another bit of industry news: James Gunn and Peter Safran's ousting at DC Studios. With Matt Reeves' two biggest champions gone, might this uncertainty have a trickle-down effect? According to Belloni, it sure could:

"Even before director Matt Reeves was temporarily replaced by Steven Soderbergh due to a personal issue, Reeves had fallen far behind on ['The Batman Part II'], which eventually pushed the release date to February 2028. It's hard to believe that Skydance, and its new DC president, Jeremy Latcham, will go down that path again. Indulging a lengthy timeline on the company's number one franchise is probably not an option for the debt-laden Skydance. And without Reeves, Pattinson is unlikely to continue in the role, I'd guess."

Walk with me on this hypothetical, folks. After sitting out much of the initial frenzy surrounding the James Bond casting, Robert Pattinson finally got the call from Amazon and/or Bond director Denis Villeneuve following the shakeup at DC Studios. Previously, Pattinson and Matt Reeves may have been planning for at least one more film to cap off the "Batman" trilogy in the years ahead — and, to be clear, this could potentially still happen. But, without James Gunn calling the shots anymore, and with Skydance CEO David Ellison itching to get his own Batman franchise underway, Reeves saw the writing on the wall and gave Pattinson his blessing to pursue a different (yet more stable) franchise lead role.

That sure sounds plausible to us, even as we're simultaneously thrilled by this Bond casting and disappointed by the possibility that "The Batman Part II" could spell the end of Pattinson's time in Gotham. So goes the reality of art and commerce butting heads in this capitalist hellscape we've made for ourselves. If this truly is the end of the road for Pattinson and Reeves' "The Batman" franchise, well, that only makes us even more excited to see the sequel arrive in 2028. Meanwhile, the trade-off will be seeing Villeneuve and Pattinson reunite after "Dune: Part Three" for what may be the most highly-anticipated Bond movie since 2006's "Casino Royale."

That's not a bad consolation prize at all. Of course, all of this is merely informed speculation, and things could always change on a dime. Stay tuned to /Film for any and all updates in the weeks ahead.

#3491. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

Curry Barker's Obsession is one of the year's best horror films, but his next movie might end up being even better. Barker is writing, directing, and starring in next year's Anything but Ghosts, and he'll be joined by a horror movie icon.

Some spoilers for The Nights Before Christmas can be found in this piece.

Hallmark is no stranger to holiday time-loop movies — the 2023 time-loop film Round and Round was my absolute favorite that year — so they definitely know how to write an effective one. Just like Hallmark Christmas movies follow a perfect movie formula, time-loop flicks also have a tried-and-true formula. A character who is unhappy in life encounters some kind of magical being or object that sets up the time loop, which they’ll ultimately spend the rest of the film trying desperately to break the curse.

Such core elements are so ingrained in the genre that it can be hard to reinvent the time-loop wheel, but by some miracle, Hallmark managed to do just that. And it totally worked!

The Nights Before Christmas premiered on the 2026 TV schedule this weekend and instantly became one of my favorite Hallmark Christmas movies of 2026. A fun yuletide flick, it follows Marty (Tyler Hynes), who is stuck reliving Christmas Eve over and over again after making a holiday wish to have more time to pursue his interests and hobbies. Marty takes full advantage of the gift of time, using it to meet people and master all his hobbies, and he seems content to keep living the same day on repeat.

Well, that is, until he meets Chloe (Laci J. Mailey), whom he feels an instant connection with. As Marty continues to repeat Christmas Eve with Chloe, he starts to wonder what his life would be like if he made it to Christmas morning.

Unlike other time-loop films, The Nights Before Christmas doesn’t start on day one of Marty’s loop. Instead, we meet Marty in one of the hundreds, if not thousands, of Christmas Eves he’s managed to live through. This is in immediate deviation from the genre that has made finding out you're in a time loop and freaking out about it one of the main features of a character’s arc. He’s also not freaked out or bothered by the sudden change in how time progresses; if anything, he welcomes and loves it.

The realization that this wasn’t going to be a day-one time loop was one that shocked me as soon as it happened, but I was totally on board with it. Admittedly, I’m not the biggest fan of the genre, so getting to watch Marty exist in the loop and be happy with his new, repetitive life was a much-needed and refreshing change to the otherwise predictable genre.

My Favorite Hallmark Christmas Movie Is Getting A Sequel, And I Can’t Wait

The film continues to reinvent the wheel as it progresses. For starters, almost every time Marty explains to Chloe that he’s stuck in a time loop, she believes him. This is unheard of with these types of films, as most of the time the stuck character has to jump through extravagant hoops to get anyone to believe and help them. Perhaps it helps that Marty isn’t asking for Chloe’s help in getting unstuck or advice on how to survive said time loop; he simply wants to spend time with her.

TNBC also finds fun ways to show the same day over and over again without long, drawn-out scenes. There’s a particularly fun sequence towards the end of the film where Marty is shown to be an excellent driver in a terrible snowstorm, despite having previously claimed to hate driving. It’s then revealed that this isn’t the first time he’s driven in the terrible storm and that the previous attempts have ended in disaster.

In its final act, the holiday film also manages to reinvent the way the time loop is resolved. All too often in these types of movies, the main characters must come to some great epiphany in order to put a stop to the loop and revert to the real timeline. This usually involves searching inward and changing something about themselves, but that’s not what happens in Nights Before Christmas. Instead, Marty discovers that he wasn’t put in the time loop to help himself, but rather he was put there to help Chloe get the Christmas she’s come to love and expect: a day with her parents. Needless to say, a narrative like this is quite refreshing in this genre.

So, if you’re a fan of time loops and Christmas, then The Nights Before Christmas needs to go to the top of your holiday watch list. The film can be streamed now with an active Hallmark+ subscription, or viewers can catch it airing on Hallmark again on Friday, November 20th at 10 PM, after the latest Countdown to Christmas lineup premiere.

#3488. Petition Demanding James Gunn And Peter Safran's DC Studios Return Passes 250K Signatures

It's true what they say: There really is nothing new under the sun. Whether it be 20, 200, 2000, or even two million years ago, humans have been behaving in surprisingly similar ways since we first figured out how to smash two rocks together and create fire. As easy as it is to believe that we're advanced and sophisticated and enlightened in all our modern sensibilities from our cave-dwelling ancestors ... well, maybe we're not so different after all, as the cliché goes.

Okay, I realize that's an unusually existential lede for an entertainment article this early in the week, but hopefully, you can see where we're going with this one. It felt like only an eyeblink ago when we were watching the #ReleaseTheSnyderCut fandom do their thing on social media in defense of Zack Snyder, the director formerly in charge of the direction of DC's movie and TV franchise. Now, his successor (and close friend) James Gunn is experiencing a similar sense of déjà vu in what has to be one of the most ironic developments in recent memory.

Only days after the news that Gunn and co-studio head Peter Safran were out at DC Studios, fans of Gunn's directorial work on 2025's "Superman" and his overall vision for the nascent DC Universe have banded together for a very familiar purpose. Yes, there's now another online movement hoping to get a major studio company to reverse course on a decision that goes up to the highest levels. A new Change.org petition titled "Keep James Gunn and Peter Safran as heads and co-presidents of DC Studios" has garnered quite a few signatures online — over 270,000, at the time of this writing.

At this rate, it's only a matter of time before somebody buys a billboard or flies a banner from a plane over Skydance HQ. While the DC Studios shakeup appeared to come as a shock to fans, it's fair to say many industry insiders figured that James Gunn's days at DC were numbered following the Warner Bros. Discovery/Skydance merger. Still, it's equally as true that neither Gunn nor Peter Safran really had much of a chance to get their rebooted universe off the ground in the first place. A solid "Superman" revival, a disastrous "Supergirl" movie, and a mid-budget "Clayface" origin story don't exactly provide a window into their plans as a whole (which reportedly spanned 10 years into the future).

Now, we'll simply have to wonder how things might have turned out in an alternate universe where the co-studio heads were allowed to cook uninterrupted.

....Unless, of course, David Ellison has his "Come to Jesus" moment as a result of some enthusiastic fans online. That raises the tantalizing question: Will this fairly sizeable petition have any effect on the wheels of machinery grinding away at Skydance? I hope any hopefuls among us are sitting down for this, because the answer is almost certainly not. But, hey, this sure beats toxic fans harassing and dogpiling and otherwise wreaking all sorts of mayhem on social media, right? (Actually, that's probably happening anyway, so scratch that.)

Even if absolutely nothing changes, the always-online Gunn can at least take some solace in knowing that many of us believe there was more to be explored with his vision of the DC Universe.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. #3486. Clint Eastwood's Frustrations With His Aerial Thriller Were Solved By A Legendary Artist

When Clint Eastwood made his 1982 jet-based thriller "Firefox," he had a great deal of trouble with the aerial special effects. The film includes many shots of high-speed aircraft, all of them filmed against sky-colored backgrounds or snowy climes, and Eastwood had trouble eliminating the hard dark matte lines that result from piecing such special effects shots together on a physical film strip. Luckily, Eastwood was able to employ John Dykstra, the Academy Award-winning special effects man from "Star Wars," to help solve the problem.

In a behind-the-scenes documentary about "Firefox," Eastwood voiced his complaints about the matte problems he had with the plane scenes in "Firefox," alluding to the fact that earthbound planes are harder to visually realize than, say, spaceships. Matte lines in starship scenes, you see, can be hidden in the blackness of space. Dykstra was also interviewed in the same documentary, and he explained that the VFX for "Firefox" were more difficult than "Star Wars" "by a factor of ten" because of the matte problem.

Dykstra was enthused to share his techniques on how he filmed the fast-streaking sky required for fast-moving plane scenes, as he was able to achieve the effect by using a very slow-motion camera — very, very slow-motion, clicking off "a frame or two" every second — while shooting footage of the sky in a Learjet that was traveling 350 miles per hour. Most film cameras shoot at 24 frames per second, so Dykstra noted that filming in such a way forced them to cover a lot of physical space very quickly.

The passing mention of a "matte line" might confuse a VFX layperson, so luckily Dykstra explained succinctly what a matte is. In Dykstra's words, a matte is "a combination of two pieces of film on to one, [to] make them look like they were shot at the same time." When two pieces of film are combined in the way Dykstra describes, a black line, or a matte line, forms around the plane or the starship in question.

"Firefox" is about a high-tech Soviet superplane, the fictional MiG-31 Firefox, that Clint Eastwood's character, Major Mitchell Gant, is enlisted to steal as part of a joint British/American military effort. /Film listed it as the seventh best of Eastwood's nine war movies, and it's definitely a must-see for any fans of the "Top Gun" films.

Naturally, a plane-based plot requires a lot of aerial scenes involving the fictional title plane that have to be inserted into shots via a matte. Eastwood recalled his VFX issues like this:

"There were so many different ways in which this plane has to fly. And the big difficulty with particular this kind of a film is, all of a sudden, you go to special effects people, and you say, 'Now, this time, we're not out in outer space where nobody knows what it looks like. We're not on a black backdrop so matte lines, etc. etc., all disappear. I want to fly in the clouds and in the planet, and I want to fly over ice, white snow, the Arctic.' And everybody's going, 'Oh my God, there's no way this is going to happen.'"

Clint Eastwood, too, seemed to be alluding to the VFX in "Firefox" in direct comparison with the effects from "Star Wars."

John Dykstra reiterated Eastwood's comment about matte lines by saying that "in space, where everything's black ... that automatically takes care of the problem." He then added that when you do a similar effect against a blue sky, "the bit that turns black between the airplane and the sky is really obnoxious." Luckily, Dykstra handily eliminated said lines using unmentioned VFX alchemy.

Elsewhere in the doc, Dykstra gave an exasperated laugh at the amount of effort that went into capturing the slow-motion shots of the sky, and how little film was used. He said:

"What we did is we went out and shot at slow framerates, meaning two frames or one frame a second. But you must remember something: one frame a second, at the speed we're traveling — 350 miles an hour in a Learjet — we cover, oh, 150 miles in the amount of time it takes to shoot ten seconds of film. So, in fact, you run out of location very quickly at that rate!"

These kinds of VFX issues were likely annoying to Clint Eastwood, as he is notoriously efficient when it comes to his directorial efforts. Eastwood saved "The Bridges of Madison County" from production limbo by essentially asking for 24 hours to begin prep. He usually gets the shots he needs in one or two takes, so his potential annoyance with the meticulous nature of having to wait for special VFX shots for "Firefox" would be understandable.

#3485. Nintendo Fans Blast New Switch 2 Release as ‘Paid Downgrade’

According to some fans, Dandori Academy gets a failing grade

So far, the Nintendo Switch 2 upgraded editions of games originally released on the Switch have been a bit of a mixed bag. While games like Kirby and the Forgotten Land received significant new content and noticeable performance upgrades, others such as Xenoblade Chronicles X weren’t quite as well received. According to many Pikmin fans, the recently released Switch 2 version of Pikmin 4 falls into the latter camp.

Pikmin 4: Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy is an upgrade for the 2023 Switch game with added levels and higher-resolution graphics. It came out last Thursday and costs $10 to upgrade from the original Nintendo Switch version. Unfortunately, the new version of Pikmin 4 currently has a dismal 1.9 out of 10 user score on Metacritic, a massive drop from the original version’s 8.9 user rating.

As for why it’s drawing so much ire, user reviews claim the Switch 2 version runs worse than it did on the previous system. Multiple players cite frame rate drops alongside longer load times. “This is essentially a paid downgrade and calling this a ‘lazy Switch 2 Edition’ or a ‘waste of money’ is an understatement for what is supposed to be an upgrade,” a Metacritic user review from PrestonandTom reads. They go on to claim that standard load times have gone from “six seconds to 30+ seconds” and that the frame rate has gone from a “consistent 30 FPS to an inconsistent 30 FPS.”

“Actively makes the game worse,” a review from Kevosan corroborates. “Longer load times than on NS1, frame drops, and glitches. The new content is NOT worth the trade-off. Standards are in the depths with this one.” Beyond the technical issues, some players also aren’t happy with the added Dandori Academy levels, which are apparently repetitive and reuse areas from the main story.

Still, there are a few upgrades that even the biggest detractors are fine with. The Switch 2 version of Pikmin 4 runs at a higher resolution, and some users commented that the voice support, which lets you give voice commands to the weird little dog-alien Oatchi, is a nice addition.

Many on the Pikmin subreddit weren’t quite as up in arms over the new version of Pikmin 4, with some saying that the negative reviews were being overdramatic. “0.6 is a score I’d only give to a game that is sub-functional,” one Redditor said about the review-bombed Metacritic page. Others argued that while the new Dandori Academy levels may reuse maps, the new enemy placements and other changes make these areas feel different.

Still, regardless of how fans feel about this upgrade, many Pikmin-heads are worried that the somewhat light changes compared to other Switch 2 editions mean that the series isn't being prioritized as highly as some of Nintendo's other tentpole releases. While Pikmin 5 hasn't been announced, at least the recently announced Pikmin shorts offer something to look forward to.

#3483. Robert Pattinson's James Bond Gives The Franchise An Opportunity It's Never Had Before

After well over a year of rampant speculation, Amazon MGM Studios and director Denis Villeneuve have found their James Bond, and it's Robert Pattinson. As many have noted, Pattinson's casting as Bond marks the first time an established movie star has been brought on to play 007 (Roger Moore and Pierce Brosnan were TV stars prior to earning their license to kill), and some folks are lamenting that the fun of a Bond transition is getting to watch an actor grow into the role. Pattinson, however, offers moviegoers a different opportunity: Just how will this actor, who's renowned for playing weirdos and affecting strange accents, approach a character who hasn't exhibited much of a sense of humor since Roger Moore surrendered his Walther PPK in 1985?

Pattinson's run as Edward Cullen in the "Twilight" movies led many to underestimate him as an actor. He played the vampire Edward Cullen as a brooding emo teenager (though he's actually 104 years old), and, at least until Bill Condon came on to direct the final two installments, the films generally didn't ask much of him. He also might've hurt himself with his portrayal of a young Salvador Dali in 2008's "Little Ashes," where his interesting physical and vocal choices are undone by a perfectly awful Spanish accent.

But once he got clear of "Twilight," Pattinson began flaunting his versatility in films like David Cronenberg's "Cosmopolis," David Michôd's "The Rover" (where he's deeply moving as a twitchy southerner who can't take care of himself), and Josh and Bennie Safdie's "Good Time" (which lets him cut loose as a low-level New York City criminal). No actor has stepped into the role of Bond with as varied a resume as this. And it only gets more varied the further along you read.

One of Robert Pattinson's zaniest performances can be found in David and Nathan Zellner's "Damsel," a dark Western comedy where he plays an eccentric pioneer who speaks in a high-pitched twang. He's an overbearing type who's not nearly as smart or entertaining as he thinks he is. Contrast this with his sublime turn as a tormented sea dog in Robert Eggers' "The Lighthouse." There, Pattinson makes for a weathered, sour delight as a lighthouse keeper who detests his tyrannical superior (Willem Dafoe) — the same chap who happens to be his only companion in this Maine lighthouse (circa 1890).

If you're looking for hints as to how Pattinson might play James Bond, he's conventionally charming and suave as agent Neil in Christopher Nolan's "Tenet," yet he plays Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves' "The Batman" as more of an aloof and dour oddball than most other actors have. If Denis Villeneuve wants a dark and brooding 007, then Pattinson's Caped Crusader might be a helpful point of reference.

For those hoping that Villeneuve might lighten up the James Bond franchise, look at his filmography. It's highly unlikely he'll let Pattinson yuk it up à la Roger Moore. But nowadays, it seems like Pattinson can't help but make interesting choices. (Just look at his 2026 trifecta of "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime.") He's one of our most interesting stars, and it would be a shame if Villeneuve played it safe and had him do Daniel Craig redux. I think that's also unlikely, but if the filmmaker could let Pattinson sprinkle some behavioral quirks into the part, we could have our most interesting Bond ... well, ever.

Johnny Depp is officially back in Hollywood, at least as far as his career is concerned. His 2026 movie release, Ebenezer, just topped the domestic box office, marking his first major studio release in eight years. But while the actor is making his way back onto movie screens (even for lesser pay), he's apparently in no hurry to return to living in the United States. In fact, he's been spending most of his time somewhere that sounds an awful lot like a vacation destination.

The Pirates of the Caribbean star recently spoke with The Wall Street Journal about his childhood, his unlikely introduction to acting and where he calls home these days. I knew Depp owned an island in the Bahamas, but I hadn't realized just how much time he actually spends there. According to the 63-year-old actor:

Today, I live most of the time in the Bahamas. It’s where I’ve found total peace and quiet. Nobody's pointing a camera at me or staring.

I suppose having your own island makes avoiding the paparazzi considerably easier. And considering how much attention Depp's personal life has received over the years, I can understand why he'd want somewhere he can go about his day without somebody pointing a camera at him.

Yet what I found particularly interesting was how the Oscar nominee described the property itself. Depp purchased Little Hall's Pond Cay, a 45-acre island in the Bahamas, in 2004 for a reported $3.6 million. And while I pictured some enormous Caribbean mansion, his description of the place sounds surprisingly modest. He continued:

I bought my 1940s wood house in 2004 and added a yurt and a painting studio. Art continues to be a sanctuary that lets me process the world around me.

A wooden house, a yurt and somewhere to paint. Not exactly what I would have pictured for the man who spent years playing one of Disney's most recognizable characters, but I can appreciate the appeal.

Depp also told the publication that he enjoys reading and playing guitar in his music studio, which sounds about right for somebody who originally moved to Los Angeles hoping to make it as a musician.

Forget Scrooge, Johnny Depp Will Soon Be Back On The Big Screen For What May Be His Scariest Role Ever

His current living situation is especially interesting considering how frequently his family moved when he was growing up. Depp recalled relocating approximately 40 times during his childhood, particularly after his family moved from Kentucky to Florida. The constant changes made it difficult to settle in, and he described himself as an outsider.

Music eventually became his escape. His mother gave him an acoustic guitar when he was 12, and by 1983, Depp had moved to Los Angeles with his band, hoping to make a career out of playing music. Then he met Nicolas Cage.

According to Depp, the two became friends after Cage started attending his band's performances. Eventually, Cage suggested that he try acting and helped connect him with an agent. That led to his film debut in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street, followed by the career that made him one of Hollywood's biggest stars.

Of course, his relationship with Hollywood became considerably more complicated in recent years. Depp stepped away from major American studio productions amid legal battles with his ex-wife, Amber Heard, including their highly publicized 2022 defamation trial. He continued working internationally, appearing in the French film Jeanne du Barry and directing Modi: Three Days on the Wing of Madness.

Now, he's back with Ti West's Ebenezer, which opened Nov. 13 and earned an estimated $19 million domestically during its first weekend. But does the box-office win signal a larger Hollywood comeback? Only time will tell, but Depp has another major American release on the horizon: Day Drinker, a thriller co-starring Penélope Cruz, arriving on the 2027 movie schedule. Still, his latest comments suggest returning to American movies doesn't necessarily mean returning to a US address.

The '80s heartthrob has owned his Bahamian retreat for more than two decades, so this isn't some sudden relocation following his Hollywood troubles. But hearing him describe how much time he spends there gives a better idea of what his life looks like these days. After years of playing Jack Sparrow, I suppose it's fitting that Johnny Depp found a little peace on an island of his own.

Ebenezer is now playing in theaters, so check your local listings for showtimes. If you want to revisit Depp's iconic portrayal of Captain Jack, all the Pirates of the Caribbean films stream with a Disney+ subscription.

#3481. Marvel’s Newest Superhero Was Created to Solve a Major Magic: The Gathering Problem

Magic's VP of design talks about Darkhold Destiny's secret new hero

Marvel has no shortage of superheroes. But when Magic: The Gathering designers started assembling the cast of Marvel: Darkhold Destiny, they discovered that even decades of comic book history couldn’t quite give them everything they needed. And what they needed was more green. The solution was to create an entirely new Marvel character.

In an interview with Polygon at MagicCon: Atlanta, Magic vice president of design Aaron Forsythe talked about the unique approach that Marvel and Wizards of the Coast are taking for the game’s third crossover set, specifically about the development of a unique character that will feature prominently in Darkhold Destiny and the accompanying Marvel Comics.

“The idea for a unique character was Marvel’s,” Forsythe says when asked outright about the new character, who is named Fraxi. “I will say that she’s a green card.”

That might sound surprising in a universe that includes the Incredible Hulk, but Forsythe meant something deeper than gamma-irradiated skin. Magic divides its characters, spells, and gameplay philosophies across five colors with distinct identities that define much of the game. Finding recognizable characters who fit green’s combination of nature, instinct, and growth can be a challenge when adapting another franchise.

“It’s a tough color in a lot of Universes Beyond sets because there are not many bestial or druidic characters,” Forsythe says. “But there are plenty of red, blue, white, and black characters throughout all sorts of IPs. Green’s always a little bit more of a stretch, the way Magic defines the ethos and power suite of green.”

In developing Darkhold Destiny, Marvel pitched the idea for the Magic team to design a unique character for the set that would join Marvel canon. In the set's unique storyline, Dormammu and Hela combine a page from the Darkhold to rip open the walls between realities, unleashing arcane nightmares across the Multiverse. Thor and Doctor Strange are positioned as the main heroes, but a third brand-new hero will seemingly join them. According to Forsythe, making that character aligned with green in the game emerged as a focus.

“That way, it would really help us flesh out our roster in a way that feels authentically Magic,” Forsythe says.

In recent weeks, listings for some Magic accessories, including a deck box and playmat, identify a character named "Fraxi, Scion of Yggdrasil." When Polygon brought up the name and suggested a connection to the World Tree, Forsythe declined to elaborate. “I will not contradict what you’re saying,” he admits.

According to a blog post from principal designer Mark Rosewater, “Scion” as part of a creature’s name essentially just means they are a “descendant” or heir of something. For someone associated with Yggdrasil, that means that Fraxi could be the World Tree’s offspring, an embodiment of its power, or someone chosen to inherit that power. None of this is confirmed by any means, but it raises interesting possibilities about the nature of Fraxi and her power. Is she the physical embodiment of Yggdrasil, created to defend the various worlds it is a part of? Is she literally Yggdrasil’s avatar, or merely a character empowered by the World Tree in the same way that plenty of other Marvel characters are chosen to wield a cosmic entity's power?

In Marvel’s cosmology, Yggdrasil is the World Tree associated with Asgard and the other realms of Thor’s mythological corner of the universe. That makes it a particularly meaningful connection for Darkhold Destiny, whose story involves an invasion across dimensions.

At an October press event attended by Polygon, narrative set lead Dillon Deveney explained that after Hela and Dormammu use the Darkhold to launch their conquest, the ensuing conflict spans more than two dozen dimensions, including the 10 realms of Marvel’s Norse mythology. A character tied to the tree connecting those realms would have an obvious stake in their survival — and potentially a useful role in defending them.

That probably feels familiar to longtime Magic players. The game’s Norse-inspired setting, Kaldheim, has its own World Tree connecting its realms. That’s distinct from Marvel’s Yggdrasil, but the shared imagery makes Fraxi’s apparent premise an especially natural fit for the crossover. Deveney’s account of her creation also suggests that her role goes beyond filling a gap in the color pie. While developing the story, he kept encountering a role that existing Marvel characters didn’t quite fit.

“There was an obvious hole,” Deveney told Polygon in October. “I found myself forcing other characters into this role.”

The team developed roughly five different character concepts and sent them to Marvel. One, Fraxi, prompted a particularly enthusiastic response.

“They came back really fast, and they were like, ‘I don’t know how you guys knew, but this one, we’ve been looking for a character like this for a while,’” Deveney recalled.

Her origin story will be told in a Darkhold Destiny comic written by Jackson Lanzing and Collin Kelly. The first chapter will be released digitally on Feb. 26, 2027, with a physical release planned to coincide with the launch of Magic's Darkhold Destiny set on April 9. For now, Fraxi looks poised to give Marvel a new connection to its World Tree — and give Magic the kind of nature-powered hero its designers were struggling to find for Universes Beyond.

#3480. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.
