#3479. The Downfall Of Sony's Spider-Man Universe Can Be Traced Back To One Moment

If Marvel Comics has proved anything over the past 63 years, it's that the number of stories you can tell about Spider-Man is essentially infinite. Not only is he a great character in his own right, he also has an incredible roster of villains and one of the best supporting casts in the history of superhero comics. And yet, despite the success of movies about the web-slinging wall-crawler himself, Sony Pictures' attempts to expand into a full-on Spider-Man Universe have been, to put it bluntly, an abysmal failure on virtually every level.

With Sony scrapping plans for expanding into more villain-focused films, moviegoers are left with burning questions. How could a cinematic franchise built around characters like Madame Web and Morbius possibly have failed? Who could have predicted that audiences might not care about the origin of Kraven the Hunter's cool jacket as much as they care about him, say, fighting Spider-Man? Was the world ever going to be ready for Morbin' Time? It's nearly impossible to say for sure, but upon examining the timeline of Sony's many attempts to get their Spidey-themed side universe going, one thing becomes apparent: It all went wrong with 2018's "Venom" — not because it was bad, but because it was good.

Under normal circumstances, a superhero movie being good would be the furthest thing from a problem, even if it might seem like an unlikely success. 1998's "Blade," after all, took its title vampire hunter from a C-list character to a surprise hit, becoming Marvel's first brush with cinematic success years before the X-Men and Spider-Man hit the big screen. That proved that with a strong enough vision, a character could be taken out of the context of a traditional story and work just as well — or in Blade's case, even better.

It's hard not to look at "Venom" as a sort of cinematic descendant of "Blade." Both movies took a darker approach to superhero storytelling and mixed in a heaping helping of genre conventions to keep things feeling fresh — vampire horror for "Blade," and classic alien invasion sci-fi for "Venom." There are, however, some pretty significant differences. For one, unlike the pre-movie version of Blade, Venom had a much stronger track record of being a fan-favorite character who could stand on his own, even with his unbreakable ties to Spider-Man. For another, while "Blade" was definitely a hit, the success of "Venom" absolutely blows it out of the vampire-infested water. Thanks largely to Tom Hardy's incredibly charismatic performance as both Eddie Brock and his alien symbiote BFF, "Venom" racked up a staggering $856 million at the box office.

"Venom" brought in a ton of money, garnered acclaim from critics and fans, and seemed to be proof of concept that characters related to Spider-Man can carry a film without him. For a company looking to build its own superhero franchise juggernaut (or at least a franchise Rhino) with a suite of characters whose rights its been hanging onto for over 20 years, that's good news, right? Well ... not if you're determined to learn the wrong lesson.

While we'll never really know what was going through the minds of the studio executives who thought releasing "Morbius" twice was a good idea, it's easy to imagine how a thought process that's more concerned with the bottom line than with storytelling and character might interpret the massive success of "Venom." If that movie can succeed by featuring a Spider-Man villain on his own without Spider-Man involved at all, then why can't all these other characters that came along when Sony got the Spidey rights? These characters are pretty much all the same, right? One's as good as any other.

Unfortunately for Sony, that's not exactly how it works. Villains, particularly Spider-Man's roster of sinister foes, are built to work in the context of their heroic counterparts, and the same usually goes for the supporting cast that orbits around them. It's the contrast and context that makes them interesting. Venom works in a starring role because he's been the protagonist of his own stories for far longer than he was a pure villain. Kraven the Hunter, on the other hand, doesn't have that development. Weirdly enough, the character who probably had the best shot at standing on their own was Morbius, who is only tangentially related to Spider-Man and has a history of starring in his own stories, albeit with very little success. Alas, it turns out that sometimes, you actually have to make a good movie, and "Morbius" is anything but that.

Of course, trying to make a Spider-Man universe without Spider-Man was only one of several baffling choices Sony made with its attempted franchise. If any executive had bothered to ask literally anyone who reads comics or knows about superheroes if they should make a movie about Morbius or Madame Web, they would've found out just from the facial expression they were met with that this was a terrible idea. Her web may connect us all, but it certainly wasn't going to connect with audiences.

As a Disneyland expert and superfan, there are a few items on my bucket list that I know I’ll probably never do. Those include dining at Club 33 and getting a chance to sleep inside Sleeping Beauty’s Castle. It turns out, there’s another thing that’s so exclusive I didn’t even know it was an option: sleep in Walt’s former Disneyland apartment over the newly updated Pirates of the Caribbean attraction.

While appearing on the orange carpet at the slime-obsessed 2026 Kids’ Choice Awards, Once Upon a Time princess and beloved Zootopia actress Ginnifer Goodwin revealed that she is one of the lucky few who have been able to cross that item off her hypothetical bucket list. And from the sound of it, it was an amazing experience! During her interview with Hollywood ReelTime, Goodwin said:

I’ve gone around the park, after midnight in like a robe and slippers.

First, Goodwin gets to play the original Disney Princess Snow White in the hit ABC drama Once Upon A Time, and then she gets to voice Zootopia's Judy Hopps, one of the most beloved animated rabbits. And now, she gets to go to Disneyland whenever she wants and get to stay the night in the park. It's not like I’m totally not jealous or anything! Seriously, though, what I love is that she can appreciate the privilege, given she's a fellow Disney fanatic. Check out this recap from her late 2025 trip to Walt Disney World Resort:

A post shared by Ginnifer Goodwin (@ginnifergoodwin)

Most Disneyland fans are likely aware of Walt’s apartment above the firehouse on Main Street, which guests previously were able to visit through a paid guided tour. However, many might not know that the space above the Pirates of the Caribbean attraction was also an apartment built for Walt and his family to stay and entertain guests at, since the aforementioned firehouse apartment was too small. Unfortunately, Disney passed before the suite was completed, and his brother opted to halt construction.

It wasn’t until 2006, when Disneyland ran the “Year of a Million Dreams” promotion, that his dreams came to fruition. Thanks to the plans Walt Disney left behind, the space was turned into a suite that was made available to a randomly selected guest of the park. When the promotion ended, it became a space only Disney elite, like Goodwin and her family, could access.

I’m All In On Zootopia Director’s Response To The Fans Who Want Romance Between Judy And Nick

Unfortunately, for me and Goodwin, the apartment of Pirates of the Caribbean is no longer an option for hosting an in-park sleepover. In 2017, the space was reimagined into an exclusive dining experience, 21 Royal. Technically, this experience is open to all guests, but it comes with a pretty hefty price tag: $18,000 for up to 12 guests. I guess that’s another item I’m definitely not going to cross off my bucket list!

From the sounds of the interview, Goodwin still has a few items on her own list that she hasn’t crossed off, like sleeping in the suite inside the castle. Considering the success of Zootopia 2, the reveal of the upcoming sequel Zootopia 3, and her love for all things Disney, I’m sure the Mouse will pull some strings and allow her access to the coveted spot one of these days. I just hope she takes lots of pictures and shares them with her nearly 450K followers.

If you’re local to Disneyland, you might be able to catch Ginnifer Goodwin enjoying the parks, but for those who aren’t, you can stream Once Upon a Time and both Zootopia films with an active Disney+ subscription.

#3477. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#3476. Guillermo Del Toro's Frankenstein Director's Cut Totally Changes The Movie With One Scene

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The Criterion release of Guillermo del Toro's "Frankenstein" includes a new "Reborn Cut" that reinserts eight minutes of footage.

Now, how much can eight minutes really change a movie, especially one that's already 150 minutes long? Quite a lot, it turns out. "Frankenstein: The Reborn Cut" completely recontextualizes Victor Frankenstein (Oscar Isaac) by featuring a young Victor (Christian Convery) secretly murdering his abusive father, Baron Leopold Frankenstein (Charles Dance).

In both versions, Victor comes to suspect Leopold let his mother Claire (Mia Goth) die in childbirth. This suspicion doesn't come to much in the theatrical cut; Victor confronts his father about it, who answers no one can conquer death, and Victor counters that he will. That night, Victor dreams of a "Dark Angel" promising him that craved knowledge. Victor's story of his childhood still ends with his father's death, but by seemingly natural causes.

The "Reborn Cut" includes additional dialogue; Victor says, to secure the Dark Angel's deal and protect his little brother William from "the Beast," he decided to kill his father. Victor mixes a poison recipe from Leopold's own medical library and drops it in his father's ear as he sleeps, like Claudius killing Hamlet's father.

Victor Frankenstein of the theatrical cut already showed an Oedipus complex, or a boy who sexually desires his mother and wants to kill his father. Goth plays Victor's mother and his coveted Elizabeth Harlander, and Victor's drink of choice is milk. Victor literally killing his father in the "Reborn Cut" completes the character's psychology. It also deepens his character in the rest of the movie as he becomes a father himself to the Creature (Jacob Elordi), whose violent revenge against Victor for abusing him now even more closely mirrors Victor and Leopold.

Nothing of this sort happens in Mary Shelley's "Frankenstein" book. Victor's childhood was already one of the biggest changes from the "Frankenstein" novel, where he says that "no youth could have passed more happily than mine." Victor's father dies at the end of the novel in grief from the Creature killing all of his and Victor's loved ones.

In del Toro's movie, Victor adores his mother, but his father is cold, concerned only that Victor carries on his legacy as a master surgeon — he strikes Victor with a cane when he fails in his studies. Del Toro refashions Frankenstein Sr. like his villain Captain Vidal (Sergi López) in "Pan's Labyrinth." Both men only see their wives as brood mares and dislike the child she already has. Both men's wives die in childbirth, and with the suggestion Vidal/Leopold allowed that because he only cared about the child's life.

Leopold's abuse infects how Victor treats his creation. Victor tries to rear the Creature, but it goes horribly wrong because he's echoing his father's parenting. In his arrogance, Victor also doesn't conceive of his creation as a child. Take his anger when the Creature cuts his hand grabbing a razor blade — is that parental concern or anger that the monster damaged his [Victor's] artistic work of surgically sculpting the Creature's body?

In another scene, the Creature recoils when Victor gets angry at him for not speaking, and Victor reacts in exasperated disbelief: "I'm not going to hurt you. I made you." It seems like he genuinely wants to be different from his father but doesn't know how to be, which is even more gutting in the "Reborn Cut" since we know that Victor hated his father enough to kill him.

If Leopold's death felt abrupt in the "Frankenstein" theatrical cut, now we know why. Victor making an explicit Faustian deal with the "Dark Angel" also makes Victor's later rage against it for supposedly betraying him more coherent, and that deal essentially extracting Victor's soul fits the Angel's Satanic visage.

The theatrical cut, though, reveals Victor as the villain more gradually. The Creature initially attacks like a "monster" but then the movie tells his side. Victor being a murderer undercuts the bait and switch; poisoning your own father, even an abusive one, as a child is an undeniable sign of a bad seed.

The sequence of events still flows either way. In both versions, Victor recounting his deal with the Dark Angel cuts to the Creature breaking free from the ice. In the theatrical cut, Victor asks "but how [will I conquer death]?" The Creature shows he found the answer. In the "Reborn Cut," Victor says he realized he had to kill his father as the Creature is coming to kill Victor, his father.

In a "Frankenstein" audio commentary, del Toro reveals he cut the sequence on the advice of his longtime pal, James Cameron. Victor killing his father doesn't just make him less sympathetic, Cameron argued, it weakens his character: "If Victor kills his father [...] he has completed his task. He avenged his mother. Why would he then embark on the quest for immortality?"

Leopold's last scene in the theatrical cut, Victor grabbing his father's cane and boasting he'll surpass him, emphasizes that quest will be Victor's revenge. I'm split on if the "Reborn Cut" is superior, but Victor killing his father is a clarifying change which makes the story and themes of "Frankenstein" hang together a little better.

#3475. The Odyssey's Most Disturbing Scene Barely Used Any CGI. Here's How They Pulled It Off.

Christopher Nolan and his team reveals how silicone, magnets, and Samantha Morton's performance brought a disturbing transformation to life.

Christopher Nolan and his team reveals how silicone, magnets, and Samantha Morton's performance brought a disturbing transformation to life.

She led them in, sat them on chairs, and blended them a potion of barley, cheese, and golden honey, mixed with Pramnian wine. She added potent drugs to make them totally forget their home. They took and drank the mixture. Then she struck them, using her magic wand, and penned them in the pigsty. They were turned to pigs in body and voice and hair; their minds remained the same. — The Odyssey, Emily Wilson translation

Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey arrives on digital, 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray on Nov. 17, giving audiences another opportunity to experience the filmmaker's ambitious adaptation of Homer's epic poem. Among the story's many memorable encounters is Circe, a powerful sorceress who turns Odysseus' men into pigs. Played by Samantha Morton, Circe is responsible for one of the film's most unsettling sequences, which involves a human head being transformed into that of a pig.

It's the kind of effect you'd assume required extensive computer-generated imagery. As it turns out, the filmmakers accomplished almost the entire transformation using practical effects, some silicone, and a few strategically placed magnets.

Speaking with Polygon ahead of the film's home release, visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson and special effects supervisor Scott Fisher explain how the sequence came together, revealing that the secret wasn't some elaborate digital trick. Instead, it was finding a way to let Morton perform the transformation herself.

I didn't understand at that point how much technology in that world has advanced.

Emma Thomas, Nolan's wife and longtime producing partner, admits that several moments in the screenplay left her wondering how they could possibly be accomplished, but the Circe sequence stood out.

"I loved that sequence when I read it, and I knew he wanted to make it feel very grounded," Thomas tells Polygon. "I knew that he wanted to try and do it with makeup effects to the extent that he could."

Thomas wasn't initially sure how that would work, particularly given the limitations she assumed existed with practical makeup effects.

"I didn't understand at that point how much technology in that world has advanced," she says.

Her confidence grew once she began meeting with the makeup, special effects, and visual effects teams, including makeup and creature effects artist Conor O'Sullivan.

"That was the point at which I really realized: Oh my goodness, these guys are gonna come up with a way that each can contribute their talents and their skills with the best of technology from within their own disciplines and make a seamless sequence."

Of course, getting there required a little trial and error.

According to Jackson, the team knew early on that the key to the sequence would be allowing Morton to physically interact with the heads and manipulate their transformation.

"We had various ways that we were gonna try and achieve that, with heads with kind of clay layers that she could manipulate," Jackson says.

They even built some of those early versions, but the results weren't particularly promising. The transformation took too long, making the effect difficult to incorporate into the scene.

"We both were looking at it and going, 'Yeah, that's not really gonna work in Chris's world,'" Jackson recalled.

Rather than abandon the practical approach, the team came up with a different solution, working alongside O'Sullivan to develop a skull beneath a layer of soft silicone skin. The idea was that Morton could manipulate the skull through the skin, physically changing the shape of the head. But O'Sullivan had another trick up his sleeve.

"Conor came up with this great idea of having it pre-broken and stuck back together with magnets so she could do whatever kind of manipulation she wanted to and just keep going," Jackson says.

The skull was already separated into pieces, with magnets holding everything together. That allowed Morton to squeeze and reshape the head as part of her performance, rather than wait for a complicated mechanical effect to do the work. And because the prop didn't require constant resetting, Morton could continue performing without interruption.

"The idea that there was no resetting, so no kind of breaking her performance, was why that scene was so compelling," Jackson says. "She just had this prop that she could really go to town on."

For an effect involving a human head becoming a pig's, giving an actor that kind of freedom might sound like a strange creative priority. But it meant the transformation wasn't simply something happening to a character through movie magic. Morton was physically making it happen.

"Ultimately, in what ended up in the film, there is very little visual effects affecting what was actually shot," Jackson says.

The visual effects team made some adjustments, including manipulating the eyeballs to make their movements more frantic. Jackson also notes that an ear transformation required combining two camera angles and slight of hand. But the majority of the sequence was accomplished in-camera.

"Essentially all our involvement was prior to the shoot, and then once the shoot happened, that was kind of it in camera," Jackson says. The visual effects team wasn't absent from the process. Its expertise helped develop the practical solution in the first place.

It's also consistent with Nolan's broader filmmaking philosophy, and the director notes that even sequences requiring visual effects benefit from capturing as much real material as possible.

"Even where we know we're absolutely gonna have to avail ourselves of visual effects, really try to give the compositors as much as possible to work with," Nolan tells Polygon. In the case of Circe's transformation, that collaboration resulted in an effect that required very little digital assistance once filming was complete.

For Thomas, the finished sequence demonstrates just how much could be accomplished when different effects departments combine their expertise. What initially seemed like one of the screenplay's biggest technical challenges became an example of practical and digital artists working together to find a solution.

And for audiences revisiting The Odyssey at home, the sequence offers something worth examining a little more closely. Beneath all that unsettling movie magic is a surprisingly straightforward idea: a silicone-covered skull held together with magnets, and an actress given the freedom to do the rest.

The Odyssey arrives on digital, 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray on Nov. 17

#3474. Marshals Season 2 Episode 6 Is Based On A Tragic Real-Life Story

"Marshals" has had its share of problems, but its latest chapter manages to deliver an emotionally powerful storyline based on a real-life tragedy. Season 2, Episode 6, "Roughstock," sees Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton investigating the death of Mo's (Mo Brings Plenty) nephew, Troy (Will Strongheart), in a storyline based on the real death of Mo Brings Plenty's 27-year-old nephew, Cole Brings Plenty.

Backing up a bit: "Marshals" Season 1 solidified why the pitched Thomas Rainwater (Gil Birmingham) spin-off needs to exist. In lieu of that series, Grimes' procedural has at least given Rainwater and the Broken Rock reservation significant attention so far. Not only that, the "Yellowstone" spin-off has tried to highlight real-life issues faced by Native American communities, such as in the Season 1 episode that saw Kayce and the Marshals tracking down trafficked Broken Rock girls. Now, Season 2, Episode 6 has gone even further by using the passing of Mo's nephew as the basis for its narrative.

Cole Brings Plenty was found dead in April 2024 near Kansas City, Kansas, having been reported missing a few days prior. An actor, Cole previously played Pete Plenty Clouds in the "Yellowstone" prequel "1923" and appeared in an episode of "The Tall Tales of Jim Bridger" and four episodes of "Into the Wild Frontier." Prior to the discovery of his body, police identified Cole as a suspect in a domestic violence incident. After the actor was confirmed as having passed away, The Johnson County Sheriff's Office determined there was "no indication of foul play." But the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe quickly demanded a "full and thorough investigation into Cole's disappearance and subsequent death." Hence, in "Roughstock," Kayce takes it upon himself to carry out such an investigation into Troy's death.

"Marshals" Season 2 started in disappointing fashion, but "Roughstock" marks its best episode yet. In this chapter, Kayce Dutton and Mo Brings Plenty search for Mo's nephew, Troy, before discovering his body at the foot of a cliff. There, a police officer dismisses the death as suicide and warns Kayce and Mo not to investigate further. They don't listen. Instead, they mount a search for more clues alongside Andrea Cruz (Ash Santos) and Miles Kittle (Tatanka Means). This leads them to a group of poachers, one of whom recalls seeing an as yet unidentified man hit Troy with a flashlight prior to his cliff fall, thus confirming there was more to Troy's passing than police claimed.

For Mo Brings Plenty, highlighting this issue of police failing to investigate the suspicious deaths of Native Americans was important, especially since he had a personal connection to the story. In a TVLine interview, the actor said he was "very thankful" to showrunner Spencer Hudnut and his writers for "Roughstock," explaining, "My brother and I shared our real-life experiences with them and explained to them what occurred, and for them to take that and then create this beautiful storyline and give us, give me the opportunity to share that, I'm just so thankful."

"Roughstock" ends with a service to Troy, after which Mo carries out his own ritual by a fire, bidding his nephew farewell before seeing a white horse appear in a field. As the actor told TVLine, "Here, he has his own moment to clear himself and to be able to see the other side. That was the symbolism of the horse. It represented the other side, and Mo knows that his nephew made it, because I know that my real nephew Cole made it."

As of now, Troy's killer remains unidentified. No doubt, the Marshals will continue to pursue justice for Mo Brings Plenty's nephew. For now, though, it's interesting to see "Marshals" take such a direct approach to representing Native Americans. "Yellowstone" featured several storylines designed to highlight issues faced by Indigenous tribes, and "Marshals" has maintained that aspect of its mothership series. But this is the first time the show has taken a real-life story and adapted it so directly. If nothing else, it adds a little more depth to a series that has thus far struggled to achieve any sense of believability.

"Marshals" has no idea what it's about, and that shows no signs of changing after the first six episodes of Season 2. Even Episode 6, its respectful adaptation of a real-life event is otherwise full of stilted dialogue and performances that leave a lot to be desired. "Roughstock" has the series' signature paroxysms of melodrama as well, such as when an Army veteran suddenly pulls a gun in a parking lot, forcing Pete Calvin (Logan Marshall-Green) and Belle Skinner (Arielle Kebel) to hurriedly diffuse the situation. It's a shame, really, given the rest of the episode does a decent and respectful job of highlighting a real-world tragedy.

Meanwhile, USA Today reports that the Johnson County Sheriff's Office claimed to have "conducted a thorough investigation" into Cole Brings Plenty's death and that the findings had been presented to the family. But Mo Brings Plenty and the family remain unsatisfied. "When the wheel of justice doesn't turn for us," Brings Plenty told the outlet, "I know it didn't for us, and I know there are a lot of families that are in the same situation as we are."

#3473. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3472. What Makes The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time So Great Anyway?

Is it just nostalgia, or is there something else?

Is it just nostalgia, or is there something else?

Spend even a little time online in gaming circles, and you'll inevitably come across claims that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the greatest games ever made. Those claims resurfaced with greater frequency with the announcement of the Nintendo Switch 2 Ocarina of Time remake and subsequent warm reception from critics. The reaction from those I know who played for the first time and enjoyed it has generally been "yes, it really is one of the greats." What there's been less of, however, is a concerted effort to explain what exactly makes it deserving of that praise. Make no mistake, it does deserve it — and not just for reasons of nostalgia. That’s because Ocarina of Time anticipated some of gaming's biggest trends, and now that those trends have spiralled out of control, the remake serves as a blueprint for good game design moving forward.

Like most video games whose stories endure, Ocarina of Time blends elements of classic narrative styles. It's a fairy tale tinged with tragedy, a coming-of-age tale, and a remix of classic archetypes all mashed up together, and it's one of the few games that uses its game-ness to help tell that story. The landscape of Link's adult life changes dramatically, in obvious ways like all his friends scattering and various tragedies befalling Hyrule's people, but also in more mundane ways that drive a sharp distinction between past and present.

Ghosts haunt Hyrule field, and new, stronger monsters lurk in places that young Link once played in safely, without a worry. Grown Link can ride a horse. He wears clothes his child self would never have managed, uses tools too big for a kid, and is a master of combat arts. Liked the slingshot? Tough luck, buddy. That's for kids. Adults use real projectile weapons. These tools and the addition of a horse to Link's circle of friends give him access to new parts of Hyrule he never could've visited as a child — partly for reasons of geography, but also for the simple fact that he wouldn't have stood a chance against an angry Gerudo in his younger days.

These changes create a satisfying sense of progression, sure, but they're also one of the only examples of a coming-of-age story told through gameplay. Normally, such tales get their message across through some personal ordeal, or cumulative learning, or a big epiphany. But Link has a limited personality, so those methods wouldn’t work here. Instead, coming of age for Link means literally navigating the landscape of adulthood and adjusting to the new opportunities and limitations it presents, while the memory of childhood is never allowed to fade. No other game combined its storytelling and interactive elements in such a way when Ocarina of Time first launched. Few have done it since, and none as successfully.

But Ocarina of Time was ahead of its time in more than just storytelling. It sits in the Goldilocks Zone between linearity and open-endedness. Ocarina won't hold your hand, but its relatively small size and contained nature mean you're bound to eventually work out the right path in a dungeon or the answer to a riddle on your own. It also means you're bound to run across some of its less immediately obvious side quests simply by chance, just from talking to people or investigating peculiarities in the environment. The lack of signposting creates an emergent feel that puts Ocarina closer to the likes of Disco Elysium than it does other action-adventure games of the '90s and, admittedly, most other rigidly designed modern games that fear you'll miss a side quest or line of dialogue if you aren't told where to look.

Ocarina’s rewards are usually small and limited, or sometimes just plain goofy. The tasks they're associated with demand comparatively little time, and the effort involved is effort engaging with the world — exploring out-of-the-way places, speaking with people, piecing together vague environmental clues — not clearing huge challenges or gathering dozens of unnecessary collectibles.

You can sell four masks from the vendor in Hyrule Castle Town and get a fifth fun-but-impractical mask for your trouble, without feeling like that reward massively disrespects your time. It's fine that the hole in the ground on Death Mountain only houses a cow (questionable from an animal ethics standpoint, perhaps, but fine otherwise) because it took you under one minute to reach this point from elsewhere on the map. The existence of a secret underground cow is reward enough in itself. The practical side of it, some restorative milk for an empty bottle, is a nice bonus. Nintendo built Ocarina of Time around curiosity and a drive for exploration. It was the pinnacle of open-ended design at the time, and a philosophy driven by fun over content is something modern game developers are only just gradually rediscovering now.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is timeless. It's a standout example of creativity in a contained scope and a rare instance where video games embrace what distinguishes them from other mediums and puts it to good use. Nostalgia might encourage fond feelings toward it, but it has a lot to offer beyond that and should serve as a guidepost for good game development moving forward.

On Saturday nights, I’d take my Nintendo 64 cartridge upstairs to Mémère’s apartment. She always knew where I needed to go next.

#3471. What Ebenezer's Box Office Means For Johnny Depp's Hollywood Future

Johnny Depp was once one of cinema's most cherished mainstream actors. From his early successes like "Edward Scissorhands" to Oscar-nominated blockbusters like "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl," he seemed unstoppable. It all came crashing down in the late 2010s but now, Depp is back with "Ebenezer." And based on the movie's early box office returns, it looks like his Hollywood comeback may be the real deal. At the very least, it's not over yet.

Directed by Ti West ("X," "Pearl"), "Ebenezer" opened to $19 million at the domestic box office, taking the number one spot on the charts. While "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office on its opening weekend, it dropped 72% for an $8.5 million second frame. That paved the way for Depp's new take on Ebenezer Scrooge to take the crown. Internationally, the movie pulled in a further $23 million, giving it a $42 million global start.

Against a reported $38 million production budget, that makes this an instant winner for Paramount Pictures, especially since Christmas movies tend to hang around during the holiday season. Not to mention that they also tend to have especially long lives beyond the box office. All of this to say, it looked like "Ebenezer" might be the box office hit that Depp's Hollywood comeback needed and it proved out.

The movie is based on Charles Dickens' "A Christmas Carol" but promises a new take on the familiar tale. "If you think you know his story, think again," the tagline boasts. It boasts a star-studded cast that also includes Rupert Grint, Daisy Ridley, and Ian McKellen, among many others.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is going to be a bigger hit than people realize, taking up a lot of oxygen this upcoming weekend. Thanksgiving brings with it even more competition from Disney's "Hexed" and "Focker In-Law." That said, if "Ebenezer" holds even decently well, Johnny Depp has a real shot at a meaningful Hollywood comeback, with some caveats.

For one, this is going to be a mid-budget, decent hit. It's going to build a bridge, but not a terribly sturdy one. After all of the fallout from the much-publicized feud between Depp and his ex-wife Amber Heard, many studios may still be reluctant to work with him. However, it's clear the general public is willing to turn up for a Depp-fronted motion picture.

All of the "Pirates of the Caribbean" movies were big box office hits. Outside of that though, it's been a long time since Depp has been a meaningful movie star. Depp proved his best days were behind him with the big box office bomb "Mortdecai" in 2015, even before his public fall from grace. His last year as a real movie star was 2017, when "Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales" and "Murder on the Orient Express" both came out.

That said, Depp was also named the most overpaid actor of both 2015 and 2016, with box office returns not matching his asking price. In light of "Ebenezer," Depp's path toward a larger comeback is somewhat narrow. He needs to be realistic about what salary he can command and to go for a sure thing. Is that a return as Captain Jack Sparrow? We'll see ... but we probably haven't seen the last of Depp, that much is certain.

#3469. These Early Black Friday Ring Camera Deals Start at $24.99

#3468. Samara Weaving's Gritty Crime Thriller Is One Of Netflix's Biggest Streaming Hits

Samara Weaving is one of the most charismatic young actresses working right now. She's got one of the most expressive acting faces this side of Saoirse-Monica Jackson in "Derry Girls," and the comic sense to know how to use it.

2026 has been good for Weaving — and not just because she booked a part as Emma Frost in Marvel Studios' upcoming "X-Men" movie. This past year, Weaving has starred in three movies. She returned for a sequel to her 2019 horror movie "Ready or Not," and co-starred with Jason Segel in "Over Your Dead Body," a comedy-thriller about two spouses plotting to kill each other (like "War of the Roses" with violence out of "Looney Tunes"). The year's third Weaving film is "Carolina Carolina," which came and went from theaters with not even $1 million to its name. But since being added to Netflix on November 6, 2026, the movie has consistently placed in the service's top 10 most viewed movies.

Directed by Adam Carter Rehmeier, "Carolina Caroline" stars Weaving as Caroline Daniels, working as a gas station attendant in Texas at the turn of the millennium. One day, the slick Oliver Anderson (Kyle Gallner) saunters in and tricks the station's cashier out of $20. Carolina, noticing the con, is nonetheless charmed by Oliver. They hit it off, him teaching her how to run short change cons, and, before long, they're driving across the American South robbing banks together. If you've ever heard the names "Bonnie" and "Clyde," then you know what to expect from this story, but familiar pleasures are pleasures nonetheless.

The engine of "Carolina Caroline" is the central criminal romance. Oliver is Caroline's teacher and her lover, and the sexiness of their romance is intertwined with the lawbreaking. The movie never forgets Oliver is the more experienced criminal, making him more ruthless. That he genuinely loves Caroline only hardens him more when facing the rest of the world, especially when their fortunes predictably take a bad turn in the third act. While Caroline is sometimes shocked by the violence, it reads more as inexperience first, conscience second.

The casting helps fuel the movie, too. It'd be overstating it to call "Carolina Caroline" a "Heat"-esque movie star collision. But both Samara Weaving and Kyle Gallner (who previously worked with Adam Carter Rehmeier in 2022's "Dinner in America") are genre favorites. Weaving is a scream queen and horror-action star thanks to "Ready or Not," while Gallner is a frequent face in horror movies, too: "Smile," the subverted slasher "Strange Darling," etc. Pair their charms together, and you never doubt for a second what draws Caroline and Oliver to risk it all in their whirlwind love story.

"Carolina Caroline" prompts comparisons to New Hollywood movies about fugitive lovers, including not just "Bonnie & Clyde" but also Terence Malick's "Badlands." Like those movies (released in 1967 and 1973, respectively), "Carolina Caroline" sets itself a couple decades in the past for a more nostalgic feeling. The movie doesn't even immediately scan as a period piece until you notice that no-one has a cell phone. With its indeterminate late 90s/early 2000s setting, "Carolina Caroline" stakes itself in the last decade that a story about criminals pulling big jobs then staying anonymous for months afterwards could happen.

"Carolina Caroline" is streaming on Netflix.

#3467. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3466. Marvel's Vision Was Originally Intended As A Revival Of A Forgotten Superhero

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Since his introduction in 2015's "Avengers: Age of Ultron," the Vision (Paul Bettany) has become one of the most enduring Marvel Cinematic Universe characters. Not even getting his vibranium head crushed by Thanos (Josh Brolin) back in "Avengers: Infinity War" stopped him from returning in the TV series "WandaVision" — in which Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen) conjures the life she wanted with Vision — and "VisionQuest," which revisits Vision's relationship with Ultron (James Spader), his "father."

Created by Roy Thomas and John Buscema, Vision debuted in 1968's "The Avengers" issue #57. Unlike in the MCU, where Ultron creates Vision's "synthezoid" body for himself before the Avengers steal it, comic Ultron (then known as Ultron-5) created Vision as a conscious being to lure the Avengers to their doom. Vision then turned against his creator, and the following issue #58 saw him inaugurated as an Avenger.

But Vision as we know him almost didn't exist. Thomas is a fan of the "Golden Age of Comics," aka the earliest period of superhero comics in the 1940s. Back then, Marvel was called Timely Comics, and its superhero stable included Aarkus, an interdimensional being named The Vision. Created in 1940 by Joe Simon and Jack Kirby (the same year that they created Captain America), the Vision debuted in "Marvel Mystery" #13. Summoned to Earth by scientist Enoch Mason, Aarkus hails from a supernatural dimension called "Smokeworld."

Originally, Thomas wanted to bring back this Vision as an Avenger, as Stan Lee and Kirby had brought back Captain America in "Avengers" #4. But Lee (without giving a reason) insisted on an android hero instead, so Thomas and Buscema created a new Vision in the image of the 1940s one. Aarkus has made occasional reappearances, but he definitely sits in the shadow of the later Vision.

Roy Thomas, who wrote "The Avengers" from issue #35 through #104, sometimes felt like he was playing in the minor leagues. Speaking to Yahoo in 2015, Thomas recounted: "Stan [Lee] kept taking Captain America, Iron Man, and Thor away from the Avengers. Every few months I would request to bring them back to the fold. I would say, 'You left me with a bunch of losers here.'"

When looking for a new Avenger, Thomas wanted to revive the Golden Age Vision because "[he] didn't like to create new characters for Marvel, because [he] wouldn't own them."

Vision's origin honored Lee's request to make the new Avenger an android, but Thomas and John Buscema's Vision still looks a lot like Aarkus. They share a mostly green color scheme, a high collar cape, a bald head, etc. Vision's intangibility powers also evoke Aarkus appearing and disappearing in plumes of smoke. There are some different details, granted. Vision has a "solar gem" on his forehead (which Thomas credits to Buscema, and which the MCU tweaked into one of the Infinity Stones), as well as red skin (unlike Aarkus' pale green).

Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter in 2015, Thomas surmised that Lee wasn't totally satisfied with the Vision, noting he disliked the hero's red color ("Red's not a good color!") and the "Vision" name. "It seems a little wimpy, but I felt Vision — it really means like a ghost or a mirage or an image," Thomas explained.

Nonetheless, history shows Vision's creation came with a huge ripple effect, reshaping "The Avengers" forever. Many of the book's core storylines go back to Vision, like his romance with the Scarlet Witch or Ultron's persistent efforts to destroy the Avengers, his son included.

Ultron debuted only a few issues before Vision, in "Avengers" #54. Issue #57 saw Vision seemingly destroy his creator, while issue #58 revealed the Avenger Hank Pym/Ant-Man had created Ultron, leading to the robot rebelling and erasing his creator's memory. Roy Thomas told Yahoo, "I knew right away [Ultron] is a character you would bring back." So he did when, in "Avengers" #66, subliminal programming inside Vision makes him restore Ultron in a new adamantium body. As for Vision and the Scarlet Witch, Thomas told Syfy in 2022 that he paired them because Vision didn't have a solo title, so Thomas had sole control over Vision's story.

If Aarkus the Vision had become an Avenger, it's plausible he'd have filled a superficially similar role on the team. Perhaps he and Wanda would've even ended up together. But he'd lack the connection to Ultron, which would diminish the villain.

In a foreword to 2015's "Avengers: Rage of Ultron," former "Avengers" writer Kurt Busiek notes the Ultron-Vision thread running through "Avengers" is a family saga. The family theme also heightens the contradictions that make Ultron more than just a killer robot. He's literally inhuman, yet he behaves more like an angry and erratic child than a cold machine, closer to Frankenstein's Creature than Hal 9000.

This makes Thomas and John Buscema creating Vision, instead of resurrecting Aarkus, a lynchpin moment of entertainment history in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Stan Lee, Thomas, and Buscema, when pumping out cheaply-printed "Avengers" comics in the 1960s and '70s, could've hardly predicted Vision would be a major character in the biggest blockbuster property ever. Nor that an entire TV series would rest on Vision and Wanda's romance, and then another on Vision and Ultron's antagonistic bond.

#3465. Star Wars: Galactic Racer Officially Getting the Feature Every Racing Game Needs

The year's best Star Wars game gets even better

Scrib doon! Star Wars: Galactic Racer developer Fuse Games announced the racing sim is getting a key ingredient next year: split-screen multiplayer. Up to four players will be able to square off on the same screen at once after the update.

"We’ve heard you!" Fuse's social media announcement begins, as the developer acknowledges this is a feature players have wanted since the game launched in early October. "A dedicated team at Fuse Games has been working hard to develop a new mode: Free Play. Choose your vehicle, character, planet, and track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local splitscreen action."

Galactic Racer launched with multiplayer modes, but they're only playable online. It's not clear if local split-screen multiplayer will also be playable in those other modes, like Podracing Tour, or if you'll only be able to enjoy split-screen gameplay in the new Free Play mode.

Star Wars fans have eaten well this year. Bit Reactor's Star Wars Zero Company brought turn-based tactical gameplay to the Clone Wars a month and a half before Galactic Racer let everyone join the Outer Rim's Galactic League.

It's one of the year's highest-rated games, and don't be surprised if Galactic Racer takes home some hardware come awards season. "The game's learning curve is steep, and there's a lot to manage and think about in a race. But boy, when you get there, the rush is unmatched. This is a game of both blistering speed and tactical nuance, where smart use of your abilities is just as important as racing reflexes. It's a deep game system, and the further you get into a run, the better and more rewarding it gets," Polygon's Oli Welsh wrote in his Galactic Racer review, where he called it "the best arcade racing game in a generation."

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is available on PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X. The Free Play mode will be added "in early 2027," according to Fuse Games' announcement.

#3464. Glenn Close Wipes Away Tears as She Gets Her Long Overdue Oscar While the Governors Awards Celebrate Indie Films

For the 17th year, the Board of Governors of the Motion Picture Academy gave out Honorary Oscars at the Governors Awards inside the Ray Dolby Ballroom in Hollywood, which Sunday night was crammed with the usual Oscar networkers. Honorary Oscar winners Ridley Scott (“Gladiator”), eight-time Oscar nominee Glenn Close (“Fatal Attraction”), and famed Disney animator Floyd Norman (“The Jungle Book”) represented the old Hollywood guard, while Killer Films’ Christine Vachon and Pam Koffler (“Carol”), accepting the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award, embodied the ongoing vitality of the independents.

It’s telling who shows up for these awards, which offer an opportunity for talent and craftspeople to appear in front of many Oscar voters (and media) at once. All week, contenders have been flowing into the city from far and wide to gather for this star-studded evening. They have hope. Or their studios are willing to spend the money to get them there. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Club Kid’ Scores Best Limited Expansion of the Year as Younger Audiences Embrace Jordan Firstman’s Oscar Hopeful Box Office: ‘Ebenezer’ Opens to Modest $19 Million, Showing Johnny Depp Is Still a Draw for the Right Price

Matt Damon, who has been working overtime this week on a series of “The Odyssey” panels (he moderated one), introduced Oscar honoree Ridley Scott and a stunning clip reel including “The Duellists,” “Blade Runner,” “Alien,” “Gladiator,” “Napoleon” and, of course, Damon’s “The Martian,” which he almost turned down because the role of an abandoned astronaut stranded in space seemed too similar to “Interstellar.” “Nobody gives a shit,” said Scott. Damon was glad he made “The Martian.” Scott, who is 88 and still working, sent his pre-recorded video acceptance from London. In it, he honored his late brother, “Top Gun” and “Crimson Tide” director Tony Scott, who died in 2012. “His great work would certainly have earned this recognition,” Scott said.

Of course, it didn’t hurt for Damon to charm the room as he vies for a Best Actor Oscar for his role as wily Odysseus in “The Odyssey.” Chairman of NBCUniversal Entertainment Donna Langley’s table was packed with Damon and fellow contenders Christopher Nolan, Emma Thomas, Tom Holland, Zendaya, casting director John Papsidera, John Leguizamo, and more.

And it didn’t hurt for John Malkovich to honor his old “Dangerous Liaisons” costar and New York theater buddy Glenn Close at the same time that he is vying for Best Actor for Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine” (Searchlight). “Numerous screenwriters and playwrights have uttered that phrase over the years: ‘made better by Glenn Close,'” he said. “Glenn’s got the goods. She can do the big stuff, the little stuff, and everything in between.” Her list is long and includes eight nominations. She broke out in “The World According to Garp,” followed by “The Big Chill,” “The Natural,” “Mars Attacks,” “Albert Nobbs,” “The Wife,” “Hillbilly Elegy,” and more. The story of casting her in “Fatal Attraction” is legendary. After the studio resisted, fearing she was too wholesome, Close insisted on auditioning and blew Paramount chief Sherry Lansing and Michael Douglas away. On Sunday, Close was visibly moved accepting her prize, wiping away tears, while acknowledging past co-stars like Robin Williams and Malkovich, and departed champions such as her “World According to Garp” director George Roy Hill. “Look George, I got one,” she said, holding her Oscar up toward the heavens.

Last year’s Honoree Tom Cruise showed up to support not just box-office disaster “Digger” ($50 million worldwide, stratospheric budget), he told me, “but everyone.” Cruise still goes to see movies in theaters, sneaking in, he said, cap lowered. When he screens in his private screening room, it’s often when he wants to scrutinize a film and play it repeatedly. For his part, Oscar-winning director A.G. Iñárritu (“Birdman”) felt “confused,” he said, by the range of reactions to “Digger” (Metacritic: 46), which is not ranking high on Gold Derby charts. Production Design and Cinematography seem to be its best shots.

The new Hollywood world order was on view. Early in the evening Langley was chatting with CAA’s Bryan Lourd but didn’t want to linger near the Warner Bros. table, where Skydance’s freshly minted Co-CEO Ynon Kreiz was eventually seated, while Denis Villeneuve presided over the “Dune: Part Three” table with Timothée Chalamet, who walked the red carpet with Kylie Jenner. Why show up? It means he’s interested in getting back into the Best Actor derby after losing back to back Oscars for “Marty Supreme” and “A Complete Unknown.” The movie is just starting to screen to meet critics’ groups’ deadlines.

Tom Quinn headed Neon’s table, which was front and center; producers David Heyman and Jennifer Fox, director Luca Guadagnino and stars Andrew Garfield and Yori Borisov represented Neon pickup “Artificial” (December 25). According to Fox, “Artificial” tested well before it was dropped by Amazon/MGM. Certainly the success of Silicon Valley documentary “You Can See Everything” (A24) bodes well. Quinn isn’t worried. And everyone has been asking Heyman about the hunt for the next James Bond. “We’ll know soon,” he said wearily. UPDATE: Indeed, Villeneuve’s “Dune: Part Three” star Rob Pattinson was announced Monday morning.

James Gray sat with his “Paper Tiger” stars Adam Driver and Miles Teller, who snuck out before the end of the show. “Fjord” star Sebastian Stan hung with his director Cristian Mungiu, who is running an English-language film festival right before Cannes in Romania.

Netflix’s Ted Sarandos and new content chief Peter Rice (who said he will not hire anyone to replace Dan Lim) commandeered several tables for its top contenders, “La Bola Negra” and “Possible Love.”

During the cocktail hour, I asked a couple of documentary branch members if still-buzzy “You Can See Everything” will land a nomination for their branch. “It’s competitive,” said one, citing “Naza” and “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” as shoo-ins. “They’ll get shortlisted.” Also in the mix is “Musk” director Alex Gibney, who flew in from Amsterdam — these days awards campaigns are international — and greeted his date, who had also flown in from Europe, musician David Byrne, who wrote a song for the movie. Gibney asked me to photograph him with his doppelganger, elegant “Wild Horse Nine” star John Malkovich. “People confuse me for him all the time,” said Gibney.

Many movie stars hugged and kissed, among them Garfield and Sophie Okonedo, who stars in two well-reviewed festival favorites this season, “Mouse” and “Clarissa.” Sandra Hüller, star of “Rose,” “Fatherland,” and “Project Hail Mary,” asked to be introduced to the belles of the Academy Ball, Killer Films producers Christine Vachon and Pam Koffler.

There was warmth in the room for Scott, Norman, and Close, but the real whoops and cheers were saved for Vachon and Koffler. Filmmaker Todd Haynes, who met Vachon at Brown, introduced the duo along with Killer Films vet and Oscar-winner Julianne Moore (“Still Alice”), who is the current frontrunner for Best Actress for Jesse Eisenberg’s musical “The Debut.”

“The Debut” opens December 11th, and will likely add to A24’s amazing year at the box office, with “The Invite,” “You Can See Everything,” “Club Kid,” “Primetime,” “The Drama,” “Tony,” and “Backrooms.”

The Killer film list is long and varied and ranges over many transgressive subjects, including “Kids,” “Boys Don’t Cry,” “Hedwig and the Angry Inch,” “Far from Heaven,” “Still Alice,” “Carol,” and their first best Picture nomination, “Past Lives.” I nabbed a t-shirt listing their films in small type at their Saturday night Soho House party, which drew an impressive crowd: Sony Pictures Classics co-chiefs Tom Bernard and Michael Barker, John Turturro, Cinetic’s John Sloss, Academy documentary branch governor Roger Ross Williams, producers Cathy Schulman and Jon Kilik, Mubi’s Laura Kim, Strand’s Marcus Hu, filmmakers Lisa Cholodenko and Wash Westmoreland, and many more. (See our Killer Films story here.) Among the many collaborators they thanked at the Governors Awards for helping them over the years was PR stalwart Jeff Hill.

It wasn’t lost on the Academy crowd that while “The Odyssey,” “Project Hail Mary” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” kicked ass at the 2026 box office, the indies are flourishing at the moment, shooting original rockets into the system. Killer Films represents that energy. “Indie films, as we’ve seen this year, are as vital as ever,” Academy CEO Bill Kramer told me. “And Christine and Pam have led the way for decades and decades, and they’ve told stories that we had not seen before, and everybody’s responding to them again and again and again. These are films with staying power.”

#3463. I’m a Deals Writer, and These Are My Top 10 Tech Deals This Week

As Lifehacker's deals writer, I'm always looking for the best bargains on TVs, speakers, laptops, and other tech. Now that it's Friday, I've gathered together this week's sales highlights, all of which I've vetted using my favorite price-tracking tools to make sure they are actually good deals.

This week, you can already feel the early Black Friday deals heating up with price cuts on the M5 MacBook Air, Bose speakers and headphones, a Samsung OLED TV, and more.

The MacBook Air with the M5 chip comes in both 13-inch and 15-inch sizes, and if you're interested in either, it's a good time to buy: Amazon is selling both right now at a $200 discount. That brings the 13-inch MacBook Air to $1,099.99 (down from $1,299) and the 15-inch MacBook Air to $1,299 (originally $1,499), reaching their lowest prices since the June price hikes.

The WH-1000XM5 headphones were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6s. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (originally $399.99). These are still incredible headphones in 2026, and with a $200 discount, they are a steal.

Bose’s second-generation QuietComfort Headphones are down to $199 from $359, saving you $160 and bringing them to their lowest price yet. Weighing around 8.1 ounces, they’re among the lightest premium noise-canceling headphones, with generously padded earcups and a cushioned headband that spreads pressure without gripping too tightly. They’re also easy to pack for travel, as the earcups fold and swivel for storage in the included hard-shell carrying case.

The Bose SoundLink Plus hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers,” and it’s down to $179 (originally $269). This is a great opportunity to snatch a quality portable speaker with a big discount.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $24.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade.

The Sony WH-CH730N are $128 (originally $179), the lowest price they've ever been. They use the same Sony Connect app as the premium headphones; as a result, you get a 10-band slider on the EQ menu, a battery care feature that extends the longevity of your battery life, 50 hours of juice, ANC, Ambient Sound (transparency mode), Multipoint to connect to two devices at once, and Bluetooth 6.0.

I got the Roborock Qrevo CurvX because it seemed like the perfect robot vacuum for me, as I have a dog, a mix of different floor types, and a gym with a workout mat, and it excels at handling them all. Amazon currently has it for $749.99 (originally $1,499.99), a 50% discount, and the lowest price it has ever been.

Samsung’s HW-Q600F soundbar is down to $379.97 at Amazon from $499.99, a $110 discount that brings it to its lowest price ever. This 2025 model sits in the middle of Samsung’s Q-Series lineup and pairs a sleek, angular bar with a subwoofer in a 3.1.2 setup. Dolby Atmos also brings a modest sense of height, and effects track cleanly from left to right. You get a graphic equalizer and sound presets for adjusting the audio to your preferences through the included remote.

The Ultimate Ears Miniroll is down to $49.99 (originally $79.99), the second-lowest it has sold for so far. It’s a small, flat, puck-shaped Bluetooth speaker that weighs just over half a pound, with a removable rubber strap you can attach to a backpack, bike handlebar, or shower caddy. Despite its size, the Miniroll can get surprisingly loud—which PCMag confirms in its review—and at moderate volume, it has enough sound for a kitchen or backyard without sounding thin. As for its battery life, you get about 12 hours of playback before it needs a charge over USB-C, while its IP67 rating protects it from dust and a brief dunk in water.

If you're looking for a premium model, Samsung’s 65-inch S90H OLED TV is down to $1,397.99 from $2,697.99 at launch, saving you over $1,000. The sale price is easier to justify when you consider that this is a new 2026 model. If the 65-inch model does not suit your space, Samsung also sells the S90H in 42-, 48-, 55-, 77-, and 83-inch versions, and those sizes are discounted as well.
