#3441. 'Avengers: Doomsday' Star Says He Was Lied to About His Next Big Role

The Avengers leader is currently starring in a holiday heist

The Avengers leader is currently starring in a holiday heist

Anthony Mackie’s Sam Wilson/Captain America will be leading the Avengers in Avengers: Doomsday, guiding Thor (Chris Hemsworth), Ant-Man (Paul Rudd), Shang-Chi (Simu Liu), and Falcon (Danny Ramirez) in the fight against Doctor Doom. But while Sam is getting a big promotion, Mackie said he was lied to about his next starring role.

Mackie plays FBI Special Agent Jack Strickland in 12 12 12, a heist thriller that premiered on Apple TV on Nov. 13. Jack’s partner was killed in a bank robbery gone wrong, and since then he’s been doggedly hunting the perpetrators, criminal mastermind Paul Galvin (Jamie Dornan), and his older brother and gunman Bobby Galvin (Jack Kesy). Jack tracked them to Zurich, where he believes they’re planning their next big job.

“This was pitched to me as ‘Imagine you in The Italian Job,’” Mackie told Polygon in a virtual interview. “I was like, ‘I’m in.’ It wasn’t that at all. They lied to me. I would have never taken this job.”

Mackie said that last part with a laugh, but he is bummed he doesn’t get to cruise around in a Mini Cooper, which is what he said makes The Italian Job his favorite heist movie. Series creators Dudi Appleton and Jim Keeble tried a different way to get Dornan into his role as the master thief, but the actor didn’t do the homework.

“Jim and Dudi sent me [a movie] that I didn’t watch,” he told Polygon. “It was French. That’s not fair. I did watch some of it. I can’t remember the name of it, but it felt removed from our show where it’s in Europe but all the main players were Americans. It felt to me not incredibly useful. I’m an Oceans 12 guy. Oceans 12, Oceans 13, and 14.”

12 12 12 takes its name from the FBI Principles of Crime, which hold that it takes 12 months to plan a high-value robbery, 12 hours to pull it off, and that law enforcement only has 12 days after the crime to successfully catch the culprits. Each episode of the show is split into three different timelines representing these periods, and filming was similarly scattered.

“It was all over the map,” Dornan said. “It was tough. You’d have days where you’d be doing scenes from different blocks, so you’d be working with different directors on one day. That’s problematic for everyone involved. That was just the situation because of the locations we were in, and the way the timelines jump around. It’s tricky. There’s a lot of needing to check in with people and track where your characters were at any given point and what had happened and what hadn’t happened. As you can imagine, it was quite headache-inducing a lot of the time. It was different from a lot of other jobs you do, which are a bit easier to track.”

Appleton and Keeble hope that structure will keep viewers on their toes, splitting more methodical planning with high-stakes action and chase scenes. The first two episodes of 12 12 12 are streaming on Apple TV now, with new episodes releasing weekly on Fridays through Dec. 25. The big Zurich heist takes place on Christmas Eve and the chase starts on Christmas Day, making it perfect holiday viewing.

#3440. James Bond 26 Breaks A 64-Year-Old Franchise Rule With Robert Pattinson Announcement

Pour yourself a Vesper Martini (shaken, not stirred, of course) and get ready to celebrate, because there is finally a new James Bond actor. Five years after No Time To Die marked Daniel Craig's final appearance with his death, and after several weeks of speculation that saw the shortlist narrowed down to three all-but-confirmed names (Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, and Josh O'Connor) and a mysterious fourth (which then turned out to be a fourth and fifth, in Nicholas Hoult and Robert Pattinson), it is indeed Pattinson who will play the new Bond.

The actor was seemingly a late entry into the contest, and eschews the notion that Amazon MGM wanted a younger take on the iconic spy than in previous iterations (Pattinson is 40, which places him directly at the midpoint of Bond actor ages). He has already, quite notably, worked with Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve, playing the villain in the upcoming Dune: Part Three, which no doubt helped in his landing the role.

The other contenders had their merits, and all fans will have had their own favorite, but Pattinson being the man selected to don the tux is both predictable, given his stature among the candidates, and quite radical, for the exact same reasons. His casting is exciting, but also goes against all notions of what a new 007 actor is supposed to be.

As late as the mid 1950s, Sean Connery, then in his mid-20s, was a struggling actor, working as an extra and having to take on other jobs. His fortunes gradually turned out throughout that decade thanks to a mix of theater, TV, and movie roles, but he was at best an up-and-coming talent, and not someone who was widely known before being cast as James Bond for Dr. No, which represented his major breakthrough.

Even then, Connery was practically an A-lister compared to George Lazenby, who was a model with no movie acting experience when he was cast as the spy for his one and only outing, On Her Majesty's Secret Service.

As if playing Batman wasn't enough, Robert Pattinson has now been confirmed as the new James Bond: here's what that means for 007 and the Dark Knight.

Roger Moore was arguably the best-known Bond actor at the time of his casting, but it was primarily as a TV star, thanks to international hits such as The Saint, Maverick, and The Persuaders. Similar can be said of Pierce Brosnan, whose TV series Remington Steele was a hit, but neither actor was remotely close to being an established movie star.

In between those, Timothy Dalton was a well-respected stage actor, but his movie career hadn't yet taken off. And most recently, Daniel Craig also had a growing reputation thanks to movies like Layer Cake, but he wasn't yet a household name.

The conventional wisdom is, to borrow from a Bond parody franchise, the suit maketh the man. That by becoming Bond, it turns these actors into genuine stars, with all of them far better known after being cast than they were before it. And while it's feasible there are some people who'll only learn that the new actor's name is Pattinson, Robert Pattinson, via Bond 26, there is no doubting that he is a bona fide movie star and absolute A-lister.

He has been in major franchises, including Harry Potter and Twilight and, oh yes, he is currently Batman. He's worked with the world's biggest directors, including a scene-stealing villain performance in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey earlier in 2026 (which may well see him land an Oscar nomination as well). He's the biggest name ever cast as James Bond in the franchise's 64-year history, and it isn't even remotely close.

It might not please everyone, especially those who apparently haven't watched a movie of his in 14 years and just mutter something about "Twilight," or those who think it should be someone lesser known. There is, perhaps, some merit to the latter point, and in watching an actor grow into the role without the same preconceived notions you might have about a particular star, but that doesn't hold true when it's a movie star as chameleonic and charismatic as Robert Pattinson (seriously, just watch his role in Tenet).

His post-Twilight career has seen him proving himself as an actor of real skill and versatility, earning indie and art house credentials to go alongside his blockbuster appeal. He is one of the finest actors of his generation and, with no disrespect to the others on the shortlist, all of whom are talented in their own right, his availability surely made it an easy choice for Amazon MGM. If you can get Pattinson for Bond, then the discussions end there.

But this is not just about talent. It's about where Bond, and Hollywood, is. It's about Amazon MGM paying billions for the rights to Bond, and then shelling out again to get full creative control from the Broccoli family. The company needs this to be a surefire hit, and while the Bond IP is strong, it's taking no risks. One of the biggest and best blockbuster directors of the 21st Century has been brought in to make it, and there's now a star attraction to match.

Pattinson is box office, as 2026 has shown. The Odyssey's billion-dollar success obviously owes more to Nolan, but The Drama making $135m worldwide on a budget of just $28m is largely down to the drawing power of him and Zendaya, and even more so Primetime's $62m (made for $14m) says a lot about "R-Pattz." And, again, he is Batman.

He's someone audiences want to turn out for, they trust him to deliver something interesting, and he has strong appeal across age-ranges, being a favorite of Gen Z - who, while again there'll no doubt be grumbles from older Bond fans, the franchise does need to attract in order to continue going, albeit without turning off those older viewers (which Pattinson's casting absolutely should not do).

Yes, the Bond name alone could carry a movie, but we aren't in the same position as, say, the 2010s, where franchises were king and that's all that mattered. Star Wars, DC, the MCU, and more have all had their struggles, while the likes of Zendaya, Timothée Chalamet, and, yes, Pattinson have seen a re-emergence of the idea a movie can be sold on the back of its star(s), something that was beginning to seem lost in such an IP-laden landscape.

In theory, then, Pattinson's casting is a perfect marriage of movie star name and household franchise, that should be a boon to both sides of the equation. And in practice, while we'll have to wait a while to find out for sure, he should be a phenomenal James Bond, and that's what matters most. It seems like a cast of right person at the right time, and there's really no reason to doubt it right now.

The James Bond franchise follows the adventures of British secret agent 007 as he combats global threats. With a license to kill, Bond faces off against various villains and criminal organizations, employing high-tech gadgets, espionage, and charm. The series spans multiple films, featuring exotic locations, thrilling action sequences, and memorable characters. Bond's mission to protect the world and uphold justice remains central, making the franchise an enduring icon in the spy genre.

#3439. Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber

This year’s TIFF and Venice were quieter in terms of breakout sales, especially when compared to last year’s splash for “Obsession,” and several awards contenders were scooped up before they even premiered at the festival. But other smaller buyers have emerged in recent weeks to release some of the more critically acclaimed titles that didn’t land major sales ahead of time.

The festivals are long done, but we’re still tracking every sale that happens, so check back frequently.

Distributor: Kino LorberDirector: Maiken BairdFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: This documentary about Palestinian-American author and intellectual Edward Said earned strong reaction in its premiere at TIFF and festivals like NYFF and IDFA, in part because though he’s been dead for over 20 years, his writing and his views have been far more relevant in a post-October 7 landscape. IndieWire’s review out of TIFF praised the construction of the documentary and how it manages to be decades-spanning and comprehensive in a manageable running time. And Anne Thompson spoke with the filmmakers about the challenges of making the documentary and the fear that it being about Palestine would pose barriers to a distributor stepping up to buy it. Thankfully, Kino Lorber did just that, and it will be planning a theatrical release for 2027. Related Stories Why Casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond Is a High-Risk, High-Reward Gamble for Denis Villeneuve ’14th’ Trailer: Ava DuVernay Unpacks the Necessity of Another Essential Constitutional Amendment

Distributor: Cohen Media GroupDirector: May el-ToukhyFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: Venice’s top prize winner of the Golden Lion has found a U.S. deal, this one made out of AFM with Cohen Media Group. Not only did el-Toukhy (“Queen of Hearts,” “The Crown”) movie win the Golden Lion this year, star Mathilde Arcel also won the Volpi Cup for Best Actress. The Danish film, also Denmark’s official Oscar selection, is a period drama set after World War II about a former housekeeper now set to be married to the household’s wealthy patriarch. But as she plans an extravagant dinner party to celebrate the occasion, hidden aspects of her past begin to resurface. Namely, it has to do with Danish witch hunts of those associated with Nazis after the war, and our positive review called it an “angry, despairing film” with a “Haneke-level bleakness in its assessment of human nature.” Cohen Media Group also recently bought an Isabelle Huppert comedy called “All About Corinne” that played at TIFF and premiered at Locarno.

Distributor: Sony Pictures ClassicsDirector: Niki ByrneFestival: TIFF Special PresentationsBuzz: Sony Pictures Classics have acquired all rights in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore) to “The Julia Set,” written and directed by Niki Byrne. The film had its world premiere at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival and follows a gifted young math prodigy (“One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti) who is “recruited into an elite prep course culminating in the most punishing exam in mathematics, while at the same time falling into a romantic relationship with her charismatic teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney).”

Distributor: Strand ReleasingDirector: Hanaël El YousfiFestival: TIFF DiscoveryBuzz: This directorial debut follows two friends, one Muslim and one Jewish, spending a carefree summer in Marseille, only to see the expectations and tensions between their traditional families start to get in the way of their friendship and leads them to take hold of their own destinies. El Yousfi both wrote and directed the feature, co-writing it with Raphaël Chevènement and Mia Grace Brown. It had its international premiere at TIFF, but it actually had a small bow at a French festival called the Angoulême Francophone Film Festival, where it won an Audience Award and a Special Prize for its cast. “The Daughters of Abraham” first opens in France on December 30. But Strand, a Culver City-based distributor behind recent releases like Mexico’s Oscar submission “On the Road,” “In a Whisper,” and the 4K restoration of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin,” will release it in North America in 2027.

Distributor: Black BearDirector: Nahnatchka KhanFestival: TIFF MarketBuzz: This market title is a rom-com starring an indelible trio of Greta Lee, Rebecca Ferguson, and Carrie Coon, and it wrapped production in September. Read more about the film here.

Distributor: 1-2 SpecialDirector: Jacqueline LentzouFestival: Venice OrizzontiBuzz: This Greek coming-of-age story won filmmaker Jacqueline Lentzou the Best Director prize in the Horizons section of the Venice Film Festival, but 1-2 Special picked it up after its North American premiere at NYFF and head of additional screenings at BFI London Film Festival, the Chicago International Film Festival, and the Busan International Film Festival. Blending what the release describes as both the “cosmic and the mundane,” the film follows a 15-year-old girl who meets a new classmate named Phaedra but also begins to notice signs and symbols from a dream world surfacing around her, ultimately leading her to an ethereal transformation. This is Lentzou’s second feature after 2021’s “Moon, 66 Questions.” 1-2 Special is planning a theatrical release for 2027.

Distributor: Sony PicturesDirector: Roshan SethiFestival: TIFF CentrepieceBuzz: This action-thriller starring Michelle Yeoh as a surgeon who is abducted and forced to operate on a mysterious patient is a bit of a departure for Sethi. Sethi’s previous film was the charming rom-com “A Nice Indian Boy,” and he’s also the co-creator of the medical drama “The Resident.” But reviews for the film were solid, and it’s not typical for the majors to buy festival titles, but Sony is already dating it for release on April 2, 2027.

Distributor: Universal Pictures and Blumhouse Atomic MonsterDirector: Joshua GiulianoFestival: TIFF Midnight MadnessBuzz: IndieWire first broke the news about the film originally set up at the Independent Film Company and Shudder being picked up by Universal and Blumhouse Atomic Monster for a deal that could surpass $10 million as the companies hope to find the next “Obsession,” just as they did last year. Read more here.

Distributor: HBO Documentary FilmsDirector: Rebecca HunttFestival: TIFF DocsBuzz: “Rapinoe” about US Women’s National Soccer star Megan Rapinoe was the opening night documentary at TIFF. Rapinoe was in attendance at the premiere screening of director Rebecca Huntt’s (“Beba”) film, which grapples more with Rapinoe’s progressive politics, such as her kneeling in solidarity with Colin Kaepernick, and her coming out story, than it does on the stories from her soccer career about how she led the US Women’s team to two World Cup titles, an Olympics Gold, and the Ballon d’Or. HBO Documentary Films has North American TV and streaming rights to the film. THR first reported the news.

Distributor: Roadside Attractions and VerticalDirector: Lauren Miller RogenFestival: TIFF Gala PresentationBuzz: Lauren Miller Rogen directs her husband Seth Rogen alongside Anna Kendrick and Kate Berlant in this comedy about parenthood and prospective parenthood. It follows a childless couple who begin debating the merits of having kids when their divorced friend and her child move in with them. The cast is stacked, including Issa Rae, Dan Stevens, Zach Cherry, Ed Helms, Ashley Park, Sharon Stone, and David Strathairn in supporting parts.

“Babies” is described as heartfelt and poignant in what is shaping up to be a strong year for Seth Rogen. The movie launched sales at TIFF nearly a year to the date prior to its Roy Thomson Hall premiere. The distributors are planning for a release in early 2027.

Distributor: Focus FeaturesDirector: Simon StoneFestival: Telluride and TIFFBuzz: Andrew Scott is said to be fantastic in this performance based on the true story of “Chariots of Fire” and “Gandhi” star and thespian Ian Charleson, who died of AIDS at the age of 40 but managed to raise awareness for the epidemic after his death. Focus has already dated the film for late November, the same time slot it gave “Hamnet” last year.

Distributor: NetflixDirector: Danny BoyleFestival: Venice CompetitionBuzz: The opening night film for this year’s Biennale, “Ink” is the story of the birth of The Sun tabloid in the ’60s and the collaboration between editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) and Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) that made it the notorious publication it is today. Netflix didn’t acquire worldwide rights to the film, so it could easily be something it sees as both commercial and an awards play.

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted home tool brand.

The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. This is one of the most versatile cordless tools, allowing you to cut a wide range of materials and use a sanding attachment to do finishing work as well.

The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. This is an excellent addition to your emergency roadside tool set because you can use it to inflate a car tire with the charged 18-volt batteries.

The Makita 18-volt cordless electric 2-inch brad nailer is on sale on Amazon for $324, 38% off its regular price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a Makita 18-volt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for attaching trim or paneling.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales on tools to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. Every now and then, a product hits the Tom’s Guide testing lab that hooks me the second I start testing it. That’s exactly what happened with the iPad mini 8.

As a 12-inch iPad Pro with M1 chip owner, three features on the iPad Mini instantly won me over: the vibrant OLED screen, the compact footprint, and the power of the A20 chip. Paired with a solid trade-in offer for my older Pro, I couldn’t resist the urge to get one for myself.

When I posted about my switch on social media, people thought I was crazy to ditch a large, laptop-replacing tablet for a smaller screen. They were wrong.

After picking up the iPad mini and using it daily for a week, I’m left asking myself why I bought the iPad Pro in the first place. The mini is, hands down, the perfect tablet for how I actually live and work.

Buying new products from Apple can get expensive, so when I saw Apple increase its trade-in values ahead of the iPad mini 8's launch, I decided it was the perfect opportunity to upgrade. Apple offered me $440 for my 12-inch M1 iPad Pro, bringing the cost of a fully specced-out iPad mini down to around $660 (without the nano-texture display).

That was the biggest selling point for me, but I could have saved even more by opting for a lower-tier configuration with the standard 128GB of storage, which would have brought my out-of-pocket cost closer to $350. Getting a new iPad with a faster processor and a better OLED display for that kind of money felt like a steal.

When I first bought my 12-inch M1 iPad Pro back in 2021, I was looking at it as a potential laptop replacement. I didn't own a MacBook at the time, so as a Windows user, the iPad became my go-to device for many of the things I now do on my Mac, including sending iMessages and making FaceTime calls.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

It's a strange thing to say, but the smaller iPad finally made me feel like I was using an iPad the way I was supposed to.

That changed when I bought a 16-inch MacBook Pro with an M3 Max chip just two years ago. Suddenly, I wasn’t on Windows all the time, and I had a much more capable laptop.

Even before that, though, the 12-inch iPad Pro wasn't exactly the most comfortable device to take everywhere. It's smaller than a MacBook, but adding the Magic Keyboard gave it some serious heft. Holding it for extended periods or balancing it on my lap to watch YouTube videos and stream movies could also get awkward. My hands would get tired, and its size meant I often needed a case just to prop it up at a comfortable viewing angle.

The iPad mini is a completely different experience. Its smaller footprint makes it much easier to use with one hand, and I can comfortably rest it on my lap while watching movies or catching up on videos. When I was playing *The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time*, on my Nintendo Switch 2 for example, it was the perfect size to keep on my lap while following online guides and navigating puzzles.

It's a strange thing to say, but the smaller iPad finally made me feel like I was using an iPad the way I was supposed to. Rather than trying to replace my laptop, it feels more like a convenient and natural extension of the Apple and non-Apple devices I already own.

In the week I've had it, I've started carrying my iPad mini everywhere. It slips easily into my bag, whether I'm using it as a second display with Sidecar or keeping it alongside my work laptop as a convenient companion device. That's something I never really felt compelled to do with my old iPad Pro.

One of the biggest reasons I was willing to give up my iPad Pro for the iPad mini was the display. The new iPad mini features a fantastic OLED panel, and my colleague Tony Polanco goes into more detail about what makes it so impressive in his review. For me, though, the upgrade was in a similar scope.

Whether I'm watching YouTube videos or streaming shows like Chicago Fire on Peacock, the iPad mini's OLED screen is a huge step up from the Mini-LED display on my older iPad Pro. While it doesn't get quite as bright, I spent enough time reviewing TVs to appreciate just how much more vibrant and color-accurate the OLED panel makes my favorite shows look.

Take Chicago Fire, for example. The flames pop with rich reds and oranges, while skin tones look noticeably more natural. Even finer details, like the soot and ash on firefighters' faces, come through with impressive clarity and depth.

That's not to say the iPad Pro had a bad display, but the iPad mini's OLED screen is simply in another league when it comes to watching movies and TV shows.

And before you ask, I really don't miss the iPad Pro’s 120Hz refresh rate. For watching videos and handling everyday tasks, the difference between 60Hz and 120Hz isn't particularly noticeable. I can spot it when scrolling through websites or swiping around the home screen, but outside of those moments, I rarely think about it.

I mentioned earlier that the iPad mini finally feels like an iPad I'm comfortable using as a companion to my other Apple devices. But out of curiosity, I decided to see how well it could handle the kind of work I used to do on my older iPad Pro. After all, with an A20 Pro chip under the hood, this is still a seriously capable tablet despite its smaller size.

Much to my surprise, the iPad mini handled it just as well as my M1 iPad Pro. When I connected it to the Apple Studio Display in our lab, I was able to arrange apps in windows and use the monitor as an extended display. I even managed to get through a full workday this way, entering data into spreadsheets in Google Sheets Chrome, responding to Slack messages, and switching between Safari and Microsoft Edge.

It's pretty remarkable that such a small tablet can handle this kind of desktop-style workflow, especially when the iPhone Duo, despite featuring the same chip, can't do the same. Considering that extended-display support and windowed multitasking were once features largely reserved for iPads with Apple's M-series processors, it's impressive to see them make their way to a smaller, more affordable tablet.

After a week with the iPad mini, I can honestly say I am glad I traded in my iPad Pro. What started as an opportunity to get a great trade-in deal turned into a much bigger upgrade to how I use my iPad.

The smaller design makes it far more comfortable to carry around and use, while the OLED display is a massive improvement for watching movies and TV shows. And despite its compact size and A20 chip, the iPad mini is surprisingly capable when I need to get some actual work done when connected to an external monitor.

Of course, there are compromises here that you’d want to keep in mind if you want to go my route. The screen is much smaller than the iPad Pro, and the lack of a 120Hz refresh rate might be noticeable for some people.

But those are trade-offs I'm more than willing to make for a tablet that's easier to take everywhere and genuinely enjoyable to use.

I bought the iPad mini because Apple's trade-in offer made it an incredibly tempting deal. But after using it for a week, I think I've discovered something more important: I just need an iPad to be a great iPad. And with that, this tiny Apple tablet is great.

#3436. Robert Pattinson as James Bond Proves That IP Is No Longer the New Movie Stars

Every James Bond casting announcement marks the start of a new era. The fictional MI6 agent has been one of pop culture’s few constants over the past seven decades; and each time a new actor steps into the role, it tells us something about the entertainment landscape we currently inhabit. Bonds can be intensely serious or silly and self-deprecating, and actors have entered the franchise at ages ranging from their late twenties to mid-forties. The role always goes to a member of the Commonwealth, but the variation that’s possible within those parameters has turned the franchise into a vertical wine tasting that illustrates what male movie stardom looks like in each decade. Related Stories Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber The Stop-Motion Tool That’s a Constant in This Crazy, AI-Mixed-Up World

The first Bond of the Amazon MGM era was destined to be even more of a turning point than usual, no matter who landed the role. The next film in the franchise will be the first one ever produced without the involvement of the Broccoli family, who have carefully guarded each iteration of the character since “Dr. No” came out in 1962. It marks the biggest movie investment that Amazon has ever made, as the tech giant spent nearly $10 billion to acquire MGM (of which Bond was the clear crown jewel) and then wrestle full control away from the Broccolis.

With Denis Villeneuve at the helm, it arguably marks the first time that Bond has been rebooted by a true auteur director with a distinct preexisting style and fan base. And it follows a Daniel Craig era that many feel took the idea of a dark, realistic James Bond to its logical endpoint with no obvious direction to go next.

When Robert Pattinson was officially announced as the seventh actor to play 007 on Monday morning, the latest era of the Bond franchise officially took shape. But it also marked the end of a larger Hollywood era in which blue chip legacy characters were seen as infinitely more important than the people playing them. We spent much of the past decade declaring that intellectual property is the new movie star(s). But casting the current Batman actor as James Bond proves that is no longer the case.

That line of thinking began to take shape in the 2010s, an era of Hollywood that will forever be defined by the phrase “cinematic universe.” As moviegoing became less of a consistent consumer habit and more of an event-driven hobby, the industry found that putting an A-list movie star or two in a new film was no longer enough to guarantee a big opening weekend. What did work, though, was slapping a Marvel logo in front of something and watching the box office dollars flow in.

Top-tier franchises were places where you went to build your star power, not cash it in. A new Bond or Spider-Man announcement was often the mainstream world’s introduction to a rising star that would be a household name within a few years. The approach was certainly better for the producers who steward these franchises: it ensured that the real value was contained in the stories and iconography that they controlled, making it relatively easy to bring in massive box office hauls with interchangeable actors who often moved onto bigger things before they became too expensive or demanding.

As that formula becomes less workable, it’s fair to wonder where we’ll start going to find our new stars. If you were casting a new Spider-Man in this environment, you probably wouldn’t pick an obscure theater actor like Tom Holland. We’re already seeing more stars come out of independent genre films, one of the few niches that can still be profitable without star power. “Obsession” gave the world its biggest breakout star of 2026 in Inde Navarette, and now she’s heading to the Marvel Cinematic Universe to help lead the “X-Men” franchise. But legacy franchises were once Hollywood’s most reliable path to minting new stars, and the industry will have to get creative if it doesn’t want the pipeline of bankable stars to fizzle out.

From an artistic standpoint, there’s every reason to believe Pattinson will make an excellent Bond. He has already worked with Villeneuve on the upcoming “Dune: Part Three” and has proven himself to be one of his generation’s most versatile leading men. He’s equally capable of playing brooding heroes and sniveling villains; a 2026 slate that includes “The Drama,” “The Odyssey,” and “Primetime” is evidence of both his range and consistent box office appeal. But from a business standpoint, it’s a decision that you wouldn’t make if you didn’t have to.

His deal reportedly costs more money for less commitment than any of the other finalists who screen tested. You’ll be juggling a production and promotion schedule that also includes “The Batman” franchise and other major films. In the run-up to the movie, more eyes will be on the man himself than the timelessness of the brand. And when the time eventually comes to replace him, expectations for the level of actor you need to land will be higher than ever before. It’s the kind of move you make when you simply cannot afford to fail. Nobody would deny that that’s the exact situation Amazon MGM finds itself in, but the mere fact that something as reliable as a new James Bond movie could place a studio in such a position is notable in and of itself.

It would be reductive to say that the pendulum has entirely swung back towards favoring movie stars. The old model where you could regularly deliver hits by putting George Clooney and Julia Roberts on a poster is certainly nowhere to be found. It might be more accurate to say that we’re in a “more is more” era of Hollywood, where no film is ever guaranteed to become the kind of cultural event that’s required to turn a profit on these massive tentpole budgets. With more competition for audience attention spans than ever before, you need to pair the power of Bond and the power of Pattinson and Villeneuve to feel truly comfortable with your investment.

#3434. The Rings Of Power Resolves Tolkien's Longstanding Ringwraith Mystery After 72 Years

Warning! Spoilers for Rings of Power season 3, episodes 1-4 ahead!It's a testament to J.R.R. Tolkien's creative mastery that all these decades later we're still obsessed with the mysteries of his fantasy world. It's been 72 years since the legendary author published The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, a work that has had a significant impact on media today. Prime Video's The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3 is an example. While the story it covers is set many thousands of years before the Fellowship left Rivendell, the narrative finds its foundation in this first of the trilogy.

It isn't long in Rings of Power season 3 before the heroes find themselves confronted by Sauron's Nazgnagôl—Ring servants. These are the early versions of the Nazgûl that were first introduced to readers in The Fellowship of the Ring. According to Tolkien, the Nazgûl were originally ordinary men who were granted the Nine Rings by the Dark Lord Sauron. These small weapons provided long life and wealth, as well as the ability to perceive the Unseen World.

This power allowed the Nazgûl to become invisible as they slipped into the parallel realm, but the power ultimately ate away at their physical forms. As they became phantoms, their minds were also tethered to the Unseen World. Tolkien explained that this process took centuries, but he never said precisely what happened from the very first moment these Men put on their Nine. This left Rings of Power with some room for creative liberties in season 3.

Rings of Power season 3 picks up five years after the end of season 2, and we see that Sauron already selected a few of his Nazgnagôl. Lucky for us, however, he isn't quite done, and we get to observe the moment that Khamûl the Easterling (one of the few canonically named members of the Nine) puts on his ring for the first time.

In Rings of Power, Khamûl suffers from a physical affliction resulting from the Dark Wizard's curses in Rhûn. When Sauron puts the Ring on his finger, we see the bloody sores covering Khamûl's body begin to fade. However, the process seems to cause the man great pain. Sauron explains that he is simply adjusting to his body's new ability to exist simultaneously in both the physical and Unseen worlds. Once this settles, Khamûl seems completely intoxicated by his new strength and power. Little does he know that over time he will lose himself entirely to a life of torment.

Tolkien's works made it seem as if the Nine had a similar impact on their wearers as the Dwarves' Seven. While the power was instantaneous, the corruption was far more gradual. This is only somewhat true for Rings of Power. We see through Theo's story that, though he wears one of the Nine, he maintains some autonomy. When he saw Arondir, he removed his mask and urged his dear friend to flee. It was clear Theo had no desire or intention of harming Arondir. However, the moment that Sauron arrived and gave the order, Theo acted.

Theo's sword went through Arondir's body so quickly that it's clear there was no option to hesitate. Theo was in control of himself, but the Dark Lord's word took that away entirely in only a moment. It's an interesting concept, and a sign that, regardless of how long someone wears one of these Nine Rings, they can't resist Sauron's direct orders while it's on their fingers. This likely has to do with the fact that these specific Rings, unlike the others, were made using Sauron's own blood. Even without the full corruption that comes over time, the Nazgnagôl are bound to their Lord.

#3433. Cary Grant, Clint Eastwood, and Christian Bale: The Stars Who Almost Played James Bond

When director Denis Villeneuve selected Robert Pattinson to play secret agent 007 in the next James Bond movie, he broke with tradition by casting an undeniable movie star in the role. Earlier Bonds were either relatively unknown (Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Daniel Craig, Timothy Dalton) or big names in television who hadn’t yet proven themselves on the big screen (Roger Moore, Pierce Brosnan). Yet Villeneuve and producers David Heyman and Amy Pascal’s choice of Pattinson isn’t completely at odds with the franchise’s history. At several points in the last 64 years, some of the box office’s biggest draws have flirted with the role and either turned it down or been rejected by the filmmakers. Related Stories Robert Pattinson as James Bond Proves That IP Is No Longer the New Movie Stars Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Edward Said: Between Worlds’ About Palestinian-American Author Lands at Kino Lorber

Right from the beginning, Bond producers were torn between going after a bankable name and letting the character be the star. Cary Grant was one of the world’s most famous actors when producers Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and Harry Saltzman began pre-production on “Dr. No,” the first feature film to showcase James Bond. (The character had previously been played by “The Shining” hotel manager Barry Nelson in a 1954 TV adaptation of “Casino Royale.”) He was also a close friend of Broccoli’s — so close, in fact, that he was best man at the Broccoli’s wedding.

Alas, that personal relationship wasn’t enough to get Grant to play Bond as Broccoli wanted. Grant was already starting to wind down his career and wanted to leave the public with their impression of him as a dashing young man. By 1966, he was done, so signing a multi-picture contract to star as Bond in 1962 didn’t appeal to the soon-to-be retired actor. Broccoli and Saltzman’s requirement that their Bond sign a long-term contract was also an obstacle for two other famous actors they approached. Both James Mason and Peter Lawford bristled at the idea of being committed to Bond for three or more films.

Rex Harrison and David Niven both wanted the part but were turned down in favor of Sean Connery, whose most prominent role to date was in the Disney movie “Darby O’Gill and the Little People.” “Dr. No” and its sequels made Connery a star, and for many viewers he remains the definitive Bond. By the time the sixth 007 movie, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” rolled around in 1969, however, Connery was tired of the role and stepped away — launching the first major search for a new James Bond.

Given that Connery wasn’t a household name when he made Bond an international icon in “Dr. No,” Broccoli and Saltzman were less inclined to go after a major movie star than they had been during the James Mason and Cary Grant discussions; most of the people seriously considered for “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” weren’t particularly popular at the time, and are even less well known now. (Few modern movie buffs would be able to pick John Richardson or Anthony Rogers out of a lineup, though the more famous Terence Stamp did meet with Broccoli about the role.)

The most popular actor Broccoli and Saltzman pursued was “Batman” star Adam West, who turned the part down because he felt 007 should be British — a response that would be repeated by other actors the next time a new Bond was needed, which turned out to be a lot sooner than Broccoli or Saltzman would have liked. Male model George Lazenby had almost zero acting experience when he secured the coveted role, but he took his good fortune for granted. In one of the great cinematic miscalculations in history, he assumed James Bond’s days were numbered in the age of “Easy Rider,” and declined to return for more 007 adventures.

Back at square one, Broccoli and Saltman decided to reverse course and once again go after big movie stars, including American ones. They offered “Diamonds Are Forever” to Clint Eastwood, who, like West, turned down the role because he felt Bond should be British. He would, however, direct and star in his own Bond-esque spy adventure, “The Eiger Sanction,” a few years later. Burt Reynolds, as famous for the hits he turned down (“Die Hard,” “Pretty Woman”) as for the ones he made, turned down Bond for the same reason.

John Gavin, best known today for his roles in Alfred Hitchcock’s “Psycho” and Douglas Sirk’s “Imitation of Life,” had no such reservations about playing Bond, and was the first American cast in the role. Unfortunately for him, Connery had second thoughts and decided to come back one last time, so Gavin was out, and Connery was in for “Diamonds Are Forever.” Gavin was briefly considered again for the eighth Bond picture, “Live and Let Die,” but by then the producers decided 007 should, in fact, be British and went with television star Roger Moore.

Moore had actually been offered “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” but had to turn it down due to an episodic series commitment. He became one of the longest-running Bonds, starring in seven 007 movies between 1973 and 1985. However, he began grumbling about leaving the series as early as 1979, leading the filmmakers to open discussions with Timothy Dalton (who turned down the role in “For Your Eyes Only” before committing to the series with 1987’s “The Living Daylights”) and James Brolin, whose bags were packed to play what would have been (again) the first American Bond in “Octopussy” when Moore had a change of heart.

The tradition of actors who either turned down or missed out on Bond in earlier films coming back to play the character was a sturdy one: just as Moore and Dalton would play the character in multiple films after initial false starts, Pierce Brosnan lost out on “The Living Daylights” due to a scheduling conflict (with his series “Remington Steele”) before replacing Dalton in 1995’s “GoldenEye.” Before the producers committed to Dalton in “Living Daylights,” a wide range of actors were considered and approached. Brosnan was the frontrunner, but Sam Neill came close, and the studio wanted Mel Gibson, but Broccoli overruled it, once again wanting a Brit (never mind the near-casting of James Brolin).

Although Brosnan was perhaps inevitable as Dalton’s replacement given the producers’ thwarted desire to have him in the 1980s, Hugh Grant, Sean Bean, and Liam Neeson were all considered for “GoldenEye.” Neeson turned the part down, later admitting that his girlfriend (and eventual wife) Natasha Richardson didn’t want him to play it. The producers wanted Bean but were overruled by MGM. Luckily for the actor, he made a strong enough impression to score a role as the picture’s villain.

Brosnan would play Bond four times, from “GoldenEye” through 2002’s “Die Another Day.” After that, the producers decided to make a change (reportedly because Brosnan’s salary demands were getting too high) and reboot the franchise with “Casino Royale.” Several now noteworthy actors were considered before Daniel Craig snared the part and became (after a brief initial flurry of internet outrage) the franchise’s most beloved Bond since Connery; Clive Owen, Sam Worthington, and Matthew Rhys were all in the running, and Henry Cavill was high on director Martin Campbell’s list.

Most intriguingly, Christian Bale turned down the part, which producer Barbara Broccoli said was his for the asking after she saw his stunning turn in Mary Harron’s “American Psycho.” Bale, amusingly, said he didn’t want to play Bond since he had already just played “a serial killer.” He also, according to the book “Christian Bale: The Inside Story of the Darkest Batman,” felt the role played into “despicable” stereotypes. Bale’s loss was Craig’s gain, as he led the Bond franchise into one of its most artistically and commercially successful periods — leaving Robert Pattinson with sizable shoes to fill.

#3432. ‘Ghosts’ Season 6 Is Taking an Unnecessary Risk With Its Release Formula

Comedy fans have been wondering when Ghosts will return for Season 6, and now they have their answer. Following a pair of holiday specials, the supernatural comedy will return in January 2027 in its usual time slot. However, there's a major change to its release schedule: the show will now air twice-weekly. In addition to its regular Thursday slot, Ghosts will also air episodes on Mondays following Eternally Yours. While this is an attempt to build a block of supernatural comedy programming, it might be a majorly wrong move on CBS's part.

For starters, shifting to a twice-weekly schedule will disrupt the series' steady momentum. Part of the fun of watching Ghosts is seeing how Jay (Utkarsh Ambudkar) and Sam (Rose McIver), alongside Kyle (Ben Feldman), run a bed-and-breakfast full of ghosts. Though the holiday specials and certain episodes have been two-part stories, they've usually aired on a single night. Shifting that status would erase the steady pacing that's made Ghosts a breakout series, and in an age when it's one of the few network series still commanding a steady audience, that could be a death sentence.

Instead of one night to sit back, relax, and catch up on new episodes, the schedule shift for Ghosts means fans risk missingan episode. That could lead to falling behind on the series and missing key developments or a genuinely funny moment — or worse, both. While streaming services have given fans more access to certain series, part of the joy of watching Ghosts lies in catching it live. Doubling the number of episodes could lead fans not only to fall behind, but eventually to skip watching altogether and wait for the entire season to drop on Paramount+.

That's a lapse that CBS can't afford. Ghosts's viewership has fluctuated over the years, as it started out strong but has decreased slightly with each season. Shifting to two episodes a week could hurt those ratings, and given that Ghosts is still one of CBS's highest-rated series, it feels like a risky gamble. Ghosts is also preparing to take some of its biggest swings yet, as Rebecca Wisocky recently told Collider that the upcoming Christmas special will be a major game changer:

"Lots of people are in peril. The stakes are perhaps the highest that they have ever been. And I don't say that lightly."

If Ghosts lives up to Wisocky's words, this won't be a season to miss. Not only will the show hit its milestone 100th episode, but the new dynamic between Jay and Kyle makes for a fresh start. Doubling up on episodes risks burning through these interesting developments, but CBS might have a good reason beyond filling up its schedule.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Some people might ask why Ghosts is doubling up on episodes, and the answer lies in another upcoming event that dominates CBS's schedule. "March Madness" will see the network air college basketball games throughout March and April, a period when multiple series usually go on hiatus until the tournament ends. If Ghosts does a double-header of its own, it could build up to a mid-season hiatus and air the rest of its episodes through May, when its season finales usually debut. This could also mark a shift back to single episodes, depending on how viewers receive Ghosts' twice-weekly episodes.

Ghosts stands out in the modern television landscape not just because it's a great comedy, but also because it sticks to a set of rules most TV shows have abandoned. It's managed to (mostly) stick to the 22-episode order that most audiences feel is outdated, and has won over an audience thanks to its mix of humor and supernatural tropes. By altering the release schedule, CBS is losing sight of what makes the series worth watching.

Seasons 1–5 of Ghosts are available to stream on Paramount+.

#3431. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3430. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3429. ‘Minotaur’ Review: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Riveting Comeback Remakes Claude Chabrol and ‘Unfaithful’ for a Hopeless Wartime Russia

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 19, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release the film in theaters Friday, November 20.]

Andrey Zvyagintsev nearly died and then came back to life in 2021 amid COVID complications, but unlike another Cannes filmmaker who resurrected from near-death only to make bad art, the Russian auteur’s riveting comeback “Minotaur” is not only a return to form — it’s also exactly the kind of hopeless, coldly gazing, and politically indicting film only the director of “Leviathan” and “Loveless” could ever make.

Based on Claude Chabrol’s 1969 erotic thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” which itself inspired Adrian Lyne’s deliciously lurid adaptation “Unfaithful” with Diane Lane in 2022, “Minotaur” follows a feckless, selfish man down a dark rabbit hole of his own digging amid the news that his wife is having an affair. We’ve seen this story before, and we know where it’s going. But Zvyagintsev, with a camera as still and gimlet-eyed as the Sphinx except when it’s gliding through the saddest rooms in the world like a seeking serpent, delivers an outcome and a movie more hopeless and on-brand than you could’ve dreamed of. His screenplay, co-written by Simon Lyashenko, is as tight as a drum, or as a rug you wrap up a dead body inside. Related Stories Cary Grant, Clint Eastwood, and Christian Bale: The Stars Who Almost Played James Bond Robert Pattinson as James Bond Proves That IP Is No Longer the New Movie Stars

Even without knowing the plot of Chabrol’s or Lyne’s film, you know everybody is doomed to their own resigned lot in life when you’re in a Zvyagintsev picture, the same director who tore an already estranged couple apart with the disappearance of their son in “Loveless,” only for the boy never to be found because, well, that’s life under Mother Russia.

But in the Russia of “Minotaur,” which was actually shot in Latvia because the days of shooting politically trenchant material in Russia are done, Gleb Morozov (Dmitriy Mazurov) is the CEO of a shipping company. He lives in a Russian suburb, ensconced from life’s daily horrors, in a modernist home made of glass, steel, fine wood, and concrete. It’s autumn 2022, and Russia is mobilizing into Ukraine, with the town’s mayor mandating that Gleb assemble a list of his employees to be drafted into service. Videos of bombings, meanwhile, are entering people’s social media feeds.

Life at home for his wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) is an empty chain of days; she’s an unemployed housewife whose existence revolves around getting their son Seriosha (Boris Kudrin) to school on time. A woman for whom getting the right presents and ordering the right food for his birthday party is a full-time job to fill the vacant space of a day. But as “Minotaur” quite quickly reveals, she’s having an affair with a 33-year-old photographer, Anton (Yuriy Zavalnyouk), whom she visits almost daily under the guise of yet another appointment. It’s something to live for, a thrilling escape from a miserable life of staring into the void, waiting for her husband and son to come home.

Lebedeva, who is astonishing here, feels less like a doomed Chabrol heroine than someone cut out of Antonioni. A forcefield of ennui with an elegant trenchcoat around her, and with the furtive glee that comes with having a secret, she makes her way a few times a week down the road to her assignations with a younger, virile artist in the sort of apartment where a woman as beautiful and rich as this would ordinarily never deign to be.

It’s no secret to the audience that Gleb, who has a history of infidelity and jealousy, is going to find out what she’s up to, nor is it a shock how he reacts. It’s mildly frustrating that Zvyagintsev, for his first film in nine years and after a brush with death, chose material that is very much familiar to his already savvy cinephile audience.

But the thrill of “Minotaur” is in how the filmmaker repositions the inevitable violence wrought from being cuckolded, the stuff we recognize from classic noir movies, into the political context of life in Russia amid its invasion into Ukraine. Imagine a Hitchcock thriller situated in the saddest, crummiest, most totalitarian corners of our times — and with an unfliching camera that offers no reassurance — and you’ll have some idea of just how bleak this unfeeling movie can get.

Mikhail Krichman, cinematographer on all Zvyagintsev’s films, returns on “Minotaur” with a glacial, widescreen gaze that encourages the viewer to examine everything around them. There’s a hypnotizing 360-shot that starts with Galina and Anton day-drinking and then getting into bed, with composers Evgueni and Sacha Galperine’s worrying score pressing upon them, only to come back to the pair in an unchanged, postcoital position. But they can’t stop what’s coming to them, which is nothing good.

Zvyagintsev loves a red herring almost as much as a cosmically depressing visual joke, like the tiny picture of Putin hanging over a boardroom. Or the detectives who eventually show up at Gleb and Galina’s house, only to later look at some serious hard evidence that could solve their wild goose case and instead think, eh, let’s just go to lunch. Or this film’s last shot, which does not leave the viewer in an easy state of mind despite the comforting falsities that its characters embrace as they float above it all.

Zvyagintsev’s latest film, like all of his others from the fraught father-son journey of “The Return” to the slinking, snaky noir of “Elena,” is devoid of easy resolution, least of all hope. It may feel too familiar to those who have followed this filmmaker’s work closely, but “Minotaur” is capable of crushing you with its final suite of images that refuse to let you forget that the world we are living in is hell.

The actors are exquisite, transcending whatever allegorical mouthpieces you might read into them as, like when Lebedeva’s Galina, absolutely wasted after not hearing back from Anton for at least 24 hours and then drinking an entire bottle of wine at a bar, berates her son and husband for ordering the same old shit for dinner every night when she’s not cooking. Margherita pizza, margherita pizza. “Where is me?” she yells at the husband she feels nothing for. The husband who has been instructing their son how to bash in the faces of bullies who come at him at school.

“Minotaur” isn’t the best movie of Zvyagintsev’s career, but the icily exacting power of his filmmaking is undeniable — and it sucks you in like a vortex. Rarely are you so glued to a tale you’ve heard so many times before. Andrey Zvyagintsev, welcome back. We missed, and we need you.

“Minotaur” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release the film later this year.

#3428. The Expanse’s Official Post-Season 6 Sequel Is An S-Tier Sci-Fi Gem

Fans of James S.A. Corey’s The Expanse know that the television adaptation, despite its success, never covered the entire original novel series. When the show concluded in 2022, many fans were left wondering what other stories the franchise still had to tell. Fortunately, after a four-year wait, fans can finally revisit that unfinished chapter with two series that, together, serve as an official, direct sequel to the television series.

The Expanse series consists of nine main novels, along with nine short stories and novellas, with Prime Video primarily adapting the first six novels for its television series. Corey's sixth book, Babylon's Ashes, provided the foundation for the show's final season. However, the seventh novel, Persepolis Rising, which Prime Video did NOT adapt, jumps approximately 30 years into the future. That's a substantial gap between the two books, but this missing chapter of the franchise's history has since been filled in with two comic-book series: The Expanse: Dragon Tooth (2023) and The Expanse: A Little Death (2025).

The end of an era is nearly here for Event Horizon, as the franchise prepares to deliever one last epic adventure, closing out its ongoing trilogy.

Together, these two series continue the story after the television show's sixth and final season, serving as official, canon continuations of the TV series' storyline. Overseen by creator James S.A. Corey and developed in collaboration with Alcon Television Group, the studio behind the television adaptation, these sequels are genuine continuations that fit into The Expanse's broader story.

With both sequels now complete, fans can binge them and discover what happens next in the franchise. Better yet, both continuations have earned exceptional reader ratings, making them worthy additions to The Expanse's legacy. For more details on what to expect from these series and where they fit within the franchise's continuity, read on.

Brought to life by superstar comics writer Andy Diggle (Green Lanterns, James Bond) and artist Rubine (Voltron: Legendary Defender), The Expanse: Dragon Tooth (2023) is a 12-part series that picks up directly after the events of the television show's final season, following the crew of the Rocinante. The series fills in the missing years between Babylon's Ashes and Persepolis Rising, exploring a previously untold chapter in the franchise's history.

In this series, fans can expect an epic expansion of The Expanse universe that dives into the secret histories of fan-favorite characters, including Holden, Naomi, Amos, and Bobbie. With this series, The Expanse's story doesn't end with Season 6; it continues in a major way. The series earned a “very positive” rating on League of Comic Geeks, with readers giving it an impressive average score of 4.3 out of 5 stars.

The Expanse: A Little Death (2025–2026), on the other hand, is a four-part canon sequel that picks up directly after Dragon Tooth. Remarkably, it received an even higher rating from fans, earning an exceptional 4.5 out of 5 stars. The series sees Andy Diggle return, this time alongside fellow writer Wes Chatham and artists Francesco Pisa and Sarah Stern.

A Little Death introduces another major adventure for Holden, Amos, and the rest of the Rocinante crew: “Following the fallout of The Expanse: Dragon Tooth, the Rocinante crew is plunged into a high stakes conspiracy when an old acquaintance of Amos Burton's comes to him for aid.” What's particularly exciting is that Wes Chatham, the actor who portrayed Amos Burton in the television series, makes his comic-book writing debut with the miniseries.

Chatham's understanding of the character shines through in this series, making it all the more special and strengthening its connection to Prime Video's show. While Dragon Tooth and A Little Death are both must-reads for fans looking to explore the missing chapter between Books 6 and 7 or continue the story beyond Season 6, there are other Expanse comics worth checking out. These include The Expanse: Origins (2020), a prequel to the television series, and The Expanse (2019–2020), a four-issue story set between Seasons 4 and 5 of the adaptation.

So, if you've been craving more of The Expanse, there's an entire comic-book universe that ties directly into the canon of the acclaimed television series, just waiting for fans to dive into.

Mighty Morphin Power Rangers fans have an epic new release to look forward to in 2027, as the classic team they fell in love with returns.

The Expanse: Dragon Tooth and The Expanse: A Little Death from BOOM! Studios is now available to read!
