#3427. 10 Classic Rock Songs That Will Make Your Thanksgiving Playlist Unforgettable

Thanksgiving means a lot of different things to different people, but there are a few universal themes that can't be ignored. There's family, there's gratitude, and there's good food. Some people will have their favorite artists to accompany them during special, but for those who are still looking for inspiration, we got you covered.

It's normal to go through many moods during a long family dinner. If you haven't seen them for a long time, it's bound to be emotional. If you're used to seeing them, chances are there will be a lot of laughter and joking around. And of course, it wouldn't be Thanksgiving without a huge dinner that leaves you panting. The Beatles, John Denver, Led Zeppelin, and many more artists and bands have created the perfect songs for your Thanksgiving playlist, and we have put them together.

We're opening this list with the most famous rock-country anthem, "Take Me Home, Country Roads," also known simply as "Country Roads." Who hasn't belted this beautiful track at the top of their lungs with a huge grin? Written by John Denver, Bill Danoff, and Taffy Nivert, and released on Denver's 1971 album, Poems, Prayers and Promises, it perfectly embodies the spirit of togetherness, gratitude, and belonging.

While it was John Denver who made it popular, the first draft of the song was originally written by Bill Danoff and Taffy Nivert. The songwriters were a couple, and were looking for a home for this song. At first, Danoff explained, they were hesitant to give it to John Denver, since they felt it might not be his style, but Denver not only loved it but helped make it into the great track it is. When asked if they regretted "giving away" their greatest hit, Danoff waved it off.

"Left to our own devices, Taffy and I may have never gotten that record cut," Danoff admitted. "It wasn't a country record. We could've beat up Nashville and nobody would've recorded it. One thing I learned in this business is that things turn out other than you planned them to, no matter what it is. And you can't predict what's going to happen." Besides, they're still credited as songwriters, so they took a big paycheck home anyway.

The title alone would earn this Led Zeppelin song a spot on the Thanksgiving playlist, but the content, despite not being strictly about the holiday, makes "Thank You" sound like it was made for Thanksgiving. It was written by Robert Plant for his first wife, Maureen Wilson. "Kind woman, I give you my all / Kind woman, nothing more," he promises in the song. "And so today, my world it smiles / Your hand in mine, we walk the miles / Thanks to you it will be done / For you to me are the only one."

Plant's relationship with Wilson is deeply romantic yet tragic. The couple were married for 14 years before splitting up, and they went through everything together. They had three children, and their middle child tragically passed away at five years old. Despite splitting up, they remained friends, and while the song might have changed meaning through the years, it never stopped being true.

The ultimate song about loving your homeland, "Sweet Home Alabama" was Lynyrd Skynyrd's response to Neil Young's songs about slavery, like "Alabama" and "Southern Man." The band felt that those songs painted an unfair picture of the modern Southern culture, so they decided to write a rebuttal about their love for their state.

"Big wheels keep on turning / Carry me home to see my kin / Singing songs about the Southland / I miss Alabamy once again and I think it's a sin, yes," the song opens. Young is even name-checked later on in the track. "Well, I heard Mister Young sing about her (southern man) / Well, I heard ol' Neil put her down / Well, I hope Neil Young will remember / A southern man don't need him around, anyhow."

But despite the diss part of the song, the underlying message is perfect for Thanksgiving. Returning to where you belong to spend time with the people you love, and being grateful for the chance to go back. "Sweet home Alabama / Where the skies are so blue / Sweet home Alabama / Lord, I'm coming home to you."

"Harvest Moon," from Neil Young's album by the same name, is one of his most famous and beloved tracks. A song about celebrating life and treasuring the time with your loved ones, "Harvest Moon" is an essential part of any Thanksgiving playlist. "Come a little bit closer / Hear what I have to say / Just like children sleepin' / We could dream this night away," he sings. It's a song about the passage of time and how love prevails, and the full moon is used as a metaphor for tradition and endurance. "Because I'm still in love with you / I want to see you dance again / Because I'm still in love with you / On this harvest moon." Perfect for the most moving moments of a family holiday, as it's guaranteed to make you reflect and appreciate your time with your loved ones more.

Another song about coming home, which is a recurrent topic for the holidays. After all, holidays are, at their core, an excuse to come home. "Homeward Bound" is one of Simon & Garfunkel's most famous songs, and partly that's because of the universal feeling of the lyrics. "I'm sittin' in the railway station / Got a ticket for my destination / On a tour of one-night stands / My suitcase and guitar in hand / And every stop is neatly planned / For a poet and a one-man band," they sing wistfully. In the song, however, the narrator is not taking the train to go home. He just wishes he was. "Homeward bound / I wish I was / Homeward bound / Home where my thought's escapin' / Home where my music's playin' / Home where my love lies waitin' / Silently for me," they sing in the chorus.

The lyrics are about a very real memory. Paul Simon remembers sitting down at a train station in Liverpool when he was just 22. A young artist trying to make his way into the world, away from home, feeling homesick. What's more relatable than that?

A classic folk rock song that is perfect for the whole family to sing along. It's pretty long, has plenty of verses, and a fun, easy chorus that makes it great to sing along to, especially later on in the evening. The most surprising thing about "The Weight" is that it was created almost accidentally. Written by guitarist Robbie Robertson, it was considered a "back-up" song, since Robertson wrote it while trying to overcome writer's block.

“I played it for the other guys, to get this thing started,” Robertson explained. “And everybody was like, ‘Hell, well that sounds pretty good!’ And I said,‘Well, it’ll just be a back-up song in case some other things don’t work out.’” To this day, it's The Band's greatest song.

"Savoy Truffle," from The Beatles' legendary White Album, is an often overlooked George Harrison composition, and it's perfect for the Thanksgiving feast. In fact, Harrison wrote it about the risks of gorging on sweets. He allegedly wrote it for his best friend, Eric Clapton, to warn him about his "chocolate addiction," and it matches the feeling of overeating during the holidays.

"Creme tangerine and Montelimar / A ginger sling with a pineapple heart / Coffee dessert, yes, you know it's good news / But you'll have to have them all pulled out / After the Savoy truffle," Harrison sings, before warning about the side effects in the bridge: "You might not feel it now / But when the pain cuts through / You're going to know and how / The sweat is going to fill your head / When it becomes too much / You'll shout aloud."

A beautiful love song, and often considered the best song by the Beach Boys, "God Only Knows" should start playing towards the moment when the family is going around sharing what they are thankful for. It's a song about appreciation and unconditional love, and it never fails to bring tears to people's eyes. "I may not always love you / But as long as there are stars above you / You never need to doubt it / I'll make you so sure about it / God only knows what I'd be without you," Brian Wilson promises on this timeless anthem.

"Two of Us" is the opening track of the controversial final album by The Beatles, Let It Be. It's a soft, upbeat folksy ballad that Paul McCartney wrote about his adventures with his first wife, Linda McCartney, and it's about exploring and having fun with your partner, and the beauty of always going home with them at the end of the day.

"You and I have memories / Longer than the road that stretches out ahead," McCartney promises in the song. "Two of us wearing raincoats / Standing solo in the sun / You and me chasing paper / Getting nowhere on our way back home."

"Our House" by Crosby, Stills, Nash, & Young is a song about domestic bliss that every young family should absolutely add to their Thanksgiving playlist, especially if it's their first time hosting. This track, written by Graham Nash, is about his love story with another rockstar, Joni Mitchell, and an epiphany he had during an ordinary day watching her pick up flowers in their garden.

"Our house is a very, very, very fine house / With two cats in the yard / Life used to be so hard / Now everything is easy 'cause of you," Nash sings happily. It's a song about the beauty of everyday things, and it's perfect for a day of giving thanks.

#3424. Best Isekai Books Like Dungeon Crawler Carl

Dungeon Crawler Carl by Matt Dinniman is not, technically, an isekai. The genre was popularized in Japan, and in the genre's current form, it centers around an ordinary person who's suddenly transported or reborn into another world. Carl isn't relocated to a different world—the madness comes to his world. But it does have all the other makings of an isekai: an ordinary dude has to go up against RPG-like elements such as monsters, leveling up, loot, questing, and so on.

Of course, there are plenty of litRPG books for fans of DCC, but there are also plenty of isekai that fans of Dinniman's books would enjoy. Lots of manga and anime play off the "adventuring in another world" trope, but we'll take a look at the light novels, specifically, which are breezy, fast-paced and fun to read bite-sized novels that are designed to be portable.

Grab one (or all) of these recommendations, because you never know when you might need some light reading when you're out and about on your own epic adventures... or just commuting to work. Plus, quite a few of these have accompanying anime, so you can continue the journey off the page, too!

In So I'm A Spider, So What? (available for purchase here) a freak accident causes an entire Japanese high school to be obliterated and killed. Most are reincarnated into another world as nobles, adventurers, and other characters. But one girl is reincarnated in a dungeon as the lowest and weakest monster of them all: a tiny spider.

Of course, part of the fun of an isekai is watching the underdog go from nothing to being kind of a big deal in the world, just like in Dungeon Crawler Carl. Over her adventures, the spider grows more and more powerful, makes some very useful allies (and, of course, some dangerous enemies), and becomes an influential figure in this strange new world.

The protagonist of Completionist Chronicles (available for purchase here) is an ordinary Joe, literally. Unlike in a traditional isekai, Joe doesn't get run over by a truck or die to get reborn. Instead, he makes a choice to permanently start over his life inside a game.

As soon as he does, Joe realizes that he has some abilities that make him a wanted man in the world. Forced to practice his forbidden magic in secret, he makes it his mission to learn more about the world. Joe won't settle for just a slight glimpse of the game; he's after that 100% completion achievement. He's going to get every item, skill, ability, and every bit of knowledge that this world has to offer, or die trying.

The Rising Of The Shield Hero (available here) follows Naofumi, just an ordinary nerdy guy who's suddenly summoned to another universe. He learns that he's one of the four legendary heroes who are destined to save the world from destruction. Unfortunately, he's the weakest and least impressive of them all: the Shield Hero.

Without a powerful weapon, Naofumi has to rely on his brains, strategies, and loyal allies who he meets along the way. Together, they fight monsters, unravel political plots, and find a way to rise above his weak-seeming shield and do his part to save this fantasy world he's found himself in.

In Dungeon Crawler Carl, Carl's survival depends largely on his use of, essentially, a hidden tool. That's also the case for Solo Leveling (available for purchase here). This series is also technically not an isekai, since Jinwoo Sung isn't transported to another world permanently. Instead, mysterious Gates suddenly appear in his world, which connect to other worlds full of dangerous monsters.

In Jinwoo's world, some people "awaken" to become fighters while others stay as weak non-fighters. Jinwoo is one of the latter. The thing is, once you awaken, you're assigned a rank, and you stay at that rank forever. One day, Jinwoo finds that he can do something no one else can: he can level up.

This changes everything. As the only person in the world who can level up and increase his strength, Jinwoo grows in power by fighting through dungeons. As he does, he uncovers the secrets of these Gates and what's happening in his world.

The idea behind Log Horizon (available for purchase here) is based around an MMORPG—a massively multiplayer online role-playing game. One day, 30,000 players wake up to find themselves trapped inside their beloved multiplayer video game, Elder Tales. The game becomes much more serious when they realize that they might be stuck in this digital world forever, with no way to escape.

A group of adventurers bands together to find a way back to their home world. They travel around the fantasy world, defeat monsters, and search for clues about what's happening. And soon, they discover something even more alarming: They respawn after death, but lose a little more of their memories each time. The fight to survive and return home begins now!

With two such similar genres as litRPG and isekai, there's bound to be some overlap. He Who Fights with Monsters (available for purchase here) sits right at that intersection between the Western litRPG and Japanese isekai.

Jason is just your run-of-the-mill office supplies middle manager until he's transported to another world. On his very first day, he has to fend against monsters, wizards, cultists, and cannibals. Like Carl, Jason has to use his wits and some special powers to stay alive in this wild world. The only problem is that he's a pretty decent guy, but all his powers are evil.

In DCC, Carl's cat Princess Donut captures the spotlight. The young cat girl in Reincarnated as as Sword (available for purchase here) is also at the center of the story, but as the title suggests, she's not the main character here.

Instead, the protagonist is an office worker who's reincarnated in the fantast world as a sentient sword. He remembers his old life, but not his name, so he becomes the girl's Teacher in both name and status. They work together to achieve both their goals: She wants to become stronger, and he wants to know why he's in this world. They learn more about themselves, too, and become an unstoppable team.

In That Time I Got Reincarnated As A Slime (available for purchase here), a guy stuck at a dead-end job meets his untimely end at the hands of a robber. As he's dying, he unknowingly makes a pact with a strange system that resurrects him in another world... as a slime, of course.

Like the spider from So I'm a Spider, So What?, the little slime doesn't stay weak for very long. He uses his special connection with the aforementioned system to acquire some extremely useful skills, then heads out on his adventure.

As the slime meets new characters, he uses his strategic way of thinking to forge some extremely powerful alliances. Just like Dungeon Crawler Carl, the slime's story revolves around a fight for survival and acquiring power. And just like DCC, the slime gets more and more involved in the overall lore and politics of the world, sending him on more epic adventures each time.

#3423. ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Returning to Theaters with a New Rosario Dawson Cameo — and Box Office Records and Oscar Noms in Mind

Usually this is the time of year when early-year and summer awards contenders come back to theaters (see: “The Odyssey”). But even though it only left theaters not long ago, Sony is re-releasing “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which is now the biggest domestic release of all time.

The studio is bringing the film back to theaters on December 4, with tickets going on sale November 19. And the new version will be an extended cut of the film (cheekily titled “Spider-Man: [Brand New] Brand New Day”) that will feature one deleted scene in which Rosario Dawson stars as a character called The Night Nurse. Director Daniel Destin Cretton had previously told press that she shot a scene for the film that was cut. Related Stories ‘Minotaur’ Review: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Riveting Comeback Remakes Claude Chabrol and ‘Unfaithful’ for a Hopeless Wartime Russia Cary Grant, Clint Eastwood, and Christian Bale: The Stars Who Almost Played James Bond

The real reason “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is coming back to theaters is because it gives the film yet another chance to add on to its record box office haul. Maybe it surpasses $1 billion domestic? It’s only $41 million shy, and the re-release of “Avengers Endgame: Encore” managed to gross $40 million domestic, so there’s a real chance of that. It also turns out that Sony really does view the film as an awards contender and thinks it deserves to be back top of mind. SPE chief Tom Rothman recently told Deadline that the studio was launching an FYC campaign for the film and believed “Brand New Day” worthy of a Best Picture nomination.

“If there aren’t people thinking about it, we’re gonna do what we can just to make people think about it,” Rothman said. “I think it’s also incumbent upon studios who make these kinds of quality commercial films to get people to think about it, and here’s what I ask people when I walk around: ‘Are you telling me that there are 10 films this year that are better than this film?’”

The only other new studio wide release on December 4 is “Violent Night 2,” so it’s a relatively light weekend in what figures to be an incredibly crowded Christmas box office, one that even includes Sony’s own “Jumanji: Open World” and of course “Avengers: Doomsday” the weekend prior.

#3421. ‘Doctor Who’ Is Officially Returning, But There’s a Catch

What does the future of Doctor Who look like? It wasn't long ago that a partnership with Disney and the return of showrunner Russell T. Davies left fans feeling as if the show's heyday was on its way back. However, this couldn't be further from the truth, as Davies' return faced poor ratings, mixed fan reception, and the controversial exit of the new titular Time Lord, Ncuti Gatwa. This all culminated in the inevitable shelving of the series, as the BBC put it out to competitive tender earlier this year.

Line of Duty creator Jed Mercurio, through his production company, Hat Trick Mercurio, looks like the favorite to take over the show, with a 2028 or 2029 return rumored. The aforementioned former showrunner, Davies, claimed that a decision on the show would arrive sooner rather than later, saying, "You’ll start to see production with a brand-new Doctor, a brand-new companion, summer next year," in a previous interview. Ahead of that confirmation, Whovians are to be treated to the big-screen return of a fan-favorite episode.

On November 23 and November 28, as part of Doctor Who Day celebrations, The Satan Pit Extended Cut hits theaters in the UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and the U.S. It was already confirmed that the new feature-length edit of the 2006 episodes "The Impossible Planet" and "The Satan Pit" will feature deleted scenes and alternate shots, but now we know that a "specially shot" sequence awaits fans.

"Before the adventure gets underway, audiences will be treated to something specially shot; a lighter, more playful moment featuring a familiar face," reads the latest publication of Doctor Who Magazine, although it is unclear who this "familiar face" is. The screening will also feature an exclusive interview with director James Strong.

The future of Doctor Who might finally be looking up, but former Time Lord Peter Capaldi isn't so positive. The Thick of It star warned in a previous interview that there is only "a small group of professionals" who could take charge of Doctor Who, and that BBC executives who "don't really understand it" threaten to lose what was once so beloved about this sixty-year-old institution. Whatever happens, Whovians will just be glad that their favorite timey-wimey series looks likely to return.

Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest Doctor Who updates.

#3420. 8 War Movie Masterpieces Praised By Real-Life Veterans

War movies movies have been a consistent genre throughout the history of cinema. Hollywood has repeatedly tapped into the stories of real-life conflicts, showing dramatized versions of what really happened. These efforts came with great rewards, too, as countless war movies have been hugely successful at the worldwide box office.

Audiences typically look for a lot of things when choosing their next war movie to watch — action, drama between characters, and potentially world-defining stakes. Yet, there’s another element that typically comes into play, too, and that is what real-life veterans think of a given film. After all, getting their stamp of approval is mightily important to any war movie, as it shows that the story they told is (for the most part) accurate to what really happened.

Some war movies have been praised for their portrayal of the conflict at hand. Andrew Garfield’s Hacksaw Ridge, which tells the story of a soldier who, due to his strong religious beliefs, opts not to carry a weapon of any kind during battle, is one war film that has been praised repeatedly. These accolades have come not only from historians who have spent their entire careers studying the conflict, but veterans who were actually there, too.

War films praised by veterans aren’t just limited to World War II, either. Movies that have centered on more recent conflicts, such as the wars in the Middle East, have also been lauded by those who served for their accuracy of their portrayal of history. Regardless, war movies remain an incredibly popular subgenre in Hollywood today, and if they’re praised by real-life veterans, then chances go up that it’s an excellent film as well.

Andrew Garfield’s Hacksaw Ridge is one war movie that has consistently been praised by real-life veterans. As stated, the film tells the story of Desmond Doss, a Seventh-Day Adventist who objected to conflict of any kind. However, when drafted into the United States military, he was forced to either forgo his religion or risk criminal punishment for not fighting.

Miraculously, Doss found a solution to this problem — not carrying a weapon at all. During combat, such as at the Battle of Okinawa (he later received a Medal of Honor for his actions during the battle), Doss had no weapons on him. He had no rifle, no pistol, and nothing that could cause harm to another human being, as Doss was adamant that he wouldn’t hurt anyone. Instead, he served as a medic, thus saving the lives of those on the battlefield, and earning a reputation as one of the bravest soldiers in history in the process.

When Hacksaw Ridge released in theaters in 2016, the question naturally arose about how much of the film’s story was accurate to real events. After all, while some war movies are based in realism, others also take plenty of story liberties. Garfield’s Hacksaw Ridge wasn’t one of these films, however, and has instead been praised by several veterans.

For example, the film’s director, Mel Gibson, showed the finished product at the Disabled American Veterans national convention in Atlanta, Georgia. The film received great applause upon its conclusion, with many veterans praising its accuracy. Dan Clare, an Iraqi war veteran, noted that Hacksaw Ridge was a surprise hit with the crowd.

“These were people who avoid war movies because they fear they will either be unrealistic or that they will trigger post-traumatic stress. To their surprise, most people felt that it was a realistic depiction of combat — one of the most accurate ever — and, by and large, they appreciated the way it portrayed PTSD. Bottom line? Unlike most Hollywood movies, this one felt like it represented us.”

Ridley Scott’s 2001 film Black Hawk Down tells the story of two Black Hawk helicopters that were shot down during the Battle of Mogadishu. Once again, this film was praised for its depiction of the battle that its based on, with many veterans who fought during this conflict noting the film’s accuracy. Not only that, but one veteran stated that “90–95% of the film” is accurate, a high number that shows just how much attention to detail went into this movie.

Another more recent title, The Outpost is based on a non-fiction book by newscaster Jake Tapper. The film tells the story of the Battle of Kamdesh and the United States soldiers stationed at the Combat Outpost (COP) Keating in Afghanistan. A fatal design flaw of the base meant that the soldiers were vulnerable to ambush from the surrounding mountains, and the film then shows their desperate fight to survive.

One of the things that makes The Outpost such a unique film is that it not only received praise from veterans, but was actually worked on by veterans, too. Director Rod Lurie is a graduate of West Point and served in the U.S. Army, and not only that, but the film also recruited several survivors from the actual events to serve as advisers on the story. This helps to make The Outpost feel raw, lived in, and true to real-life events.

Another recent film with plenty of veteran involvement is Warfare, which tells the story of an encounter that a group of Marines had shortly after the Battle of Ramadi in 2006. Interestingly, the film is told in real time, with each second passing at the same rate for both the audience and the characters. Not only that, but the script was also based solely on personal accounts that survivors gave after the attack occurred.

These methods were praised by veterans, including survivors, for adding to the film’s overall authenticity. In particular, veterans praised the “smaller moments” for depicting the quiet moments of battle, which many war films skip over. The performances of the cast were also praised, as actors like Joseph Quinn and Will Poulter did extensive research to make their portrayals as accurate as possible.

One of the earliest films on this list is The Best Years of Our Lives, which released just one year after the conclusion of World War II, in 1946. The film tells the story of three United States soldiers who return to their small towns after serving, but find the transition back to civilian life especially difficult. For example, Al Stephenson (played by Frederic March) struggles with alcoholism upon his return and, at the same time, also has a very difficult job at a bank, in which he is given the task of approving or denying loans for fellow veterans.

The Best Years of Our Lives is timeless in this regard. The film may focus on World War II veterans, but it can just as easily translate to virtually every conflict in modern human history, with soldiers struggling to find their footing after returning home. The realistic-ness of this portrayal was praised by veterans upon its release, many of whom felt seen by the film. Amazingly, many of the film’s actors were veterans themselves, including Harold Russell, who, just like his character, lost both his hands during the war.

The head of Veterans Affairs at the time, General Omar Bradley, praised this film upon its release. In fact, he was such a fan of the movie that he organized a showing for VA headquarters staff, and later went on to write to the film’s producer to express his appreciation.

Steven Spielberg has directed so many iconic films in his career, and Saving Private Ryan is right up there among the very best. The film, which released in 1998, tells the story of a battalion of U.S. soldiers who set out on a mission to rescue Private James Francis Ryan (after his brothers had already tragically been lost in battle). Tom Hanks plays Captain John Miller, the leader of the rescue mission, and Matt Damon takes on the role of Private Ryan.

Many World War II veterans, some of whom actually fought in the specific battles that Saving Private Ryan depicts, praised Spielberg’s film. D-Day veterans noted that the Omaha Beach sequence captured the true violence of the war, with paratrooper Jack Evans saying: “A lot of people will see this and think it's gruesome, but that's the way it was. There were a lot of times it was a lot worse."

One of the most recent films on this list, Atonement tells the true story of a deadly battle during the Iraq War and its longstanding aftermath. Starring Kenneth Branagh and Boyd Holbrook, Atonement begins with an extended sequence showing American soldiers patrolling the streets of a populated Iraqi village. They hear gunfire, however, and this quickly sends them into action.

On the civilian side of things, an Iraqi family similarly hears the gunfire and decides to make a run for it and escape to their hometown. What happens, though, ends up being a tragedy in every sense of the word, as the family is caught in the crossfire between Iraqi militants and the U.S. Army. Their attempts to inform the latter that they aren’t a threat prove to be fatal, however, as several of the family members are killed by U.S. soldiers, who mistakenly think of them as a threat.

Atonement is based directly not just on real events, but on real people, too. The Khachaturian family were the ones impacted by this tragedy, and Boyd Holbrook’s Lou D'Alessandro was (one of) the real soldiers in question. Meanwhile, Kenneth Branagh’s Michael Reid was the journalist who covered the events (and who facilitated a meeting between both parties years later).

When the film premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival in September, director Reed Van Dyk stated that he wanted to honor those in this story by depicting the events as accurately as possible. During the Q&A after the film’s premiere, Van Dyk noted that he and his team had received the stamp of approval from veterans who served during the War in Iraq, with particular praise going to the intensity of the combat sequence that then sets up the rest of the movie.

The 1993 film Gettysburg tells the story of the Battle of Gettysburg during the American Civil War in the mid-1800s. The film, which is written and directed by Ronald F. Maxwell, was originally filmed as a miniseries but was released for a limited run in theaters after positive reception. Because of this, it remains the longest film released in theaters in U.S. history.

Because of how long ago this war was, no direct veterans were around to see this movie. However, veterans of future conflicts noted that Gettysburg has a surprising commitment to depicting all aspects of war. Not only that, but historians praised Maxwell for including real battlefield formations, re-enactors, and for filming near the real locations where key battles took place.

#3419. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

#3418. ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

A very successful “values-based entertainment” company that was begat — in the parlance of its biblical heritage — from a film-filtering service that illegally edited “objectionable content” out of major Hollywood movies, Angel Studios has since become the world’s foremost purveyor of megachurch-approved multiplex content. The bigger they got (on the strength of projects like “The Chosen” and the QAnon cause célèbre “Sound of Freedom,” the latter of which pioneered a questionable ticketing model that continues today), the more that Angel removed from the films they released. Not just sex and swear words, but also anything that even vaguely resembled a soul. Related Stories ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Returning to Theaters with a New Rosario Dawson Cameo — and Box Office Records and Oscar Noms in Mind ‘Minotaur’ Review: Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Riveting Comeback Remakes Claude Chabrol and ‘Unfaithful’ for a Hopeless Wartime Russia

With “Hershey,” a decidedly vanilla biopic about the most famous chocolatier who’s ever lived, the studio has taken its socio-religious project to its logical conclusion: They’ve made a movie that’s been stripped of any flavor whatsoever. It’s the cinematic equivalent of carob powder. It’s what Ned Flanders will force his kids to watch next Halloween.

Somehow unimaginatively bland and Splenda-sweet all at once, this godforsaken affront to good storytelling may not have benefited from any of the material that its distributor has deemed amoral, but “Hershey” is so mind-numbingly absent the most basic friction of the human experience that I wanted to fall to my knees and thank the lord that a few errant Kisses made it past The Angel Promise on a technicality. It’s too bad Milton S. Hershey never used his platform to baselessly sow doubt in a foreign election, because at least one of Angel Studios’ co-founders would clearly have been cool with including that (ecocidal fascism is fine, just don’t say “fuck” while you’re razing the Amazon, as that would offend Jesus).

As you may have gathered by now, I am probably not the target audience for this unrepentant godslop.

Not because I’m agnostic (“Hershey” is as secular as Angel Studios’ output gets, its overt religiosity limited to a brief scene in which the movie’s namesake pleads for help from an unspecified higher power), but rather because I stubbornly, blasphemously insist that a womb-to-tomb biopic should bear at least some faint resemblance to the stuff of real life. I couldn’t possibly care less about the facts (though I struggle to believe that Hershey and his wife literally danced with joy after learning that a twist of fate had spared them from being aboard the Titanic), but there isn’t a single moment in this film that feels like it was written by a real person, let alone lived by one.

Let’s back up a beat. To be clear, Angel Studios didn’t technically make this movie — that distinction belongs to the spiritually aligned production company Dandelion Media, who partnered with Hershey Entities for a fully authorized feature-length commercial meant to “bring [the chocolate brand’s] story into culture in a more immersive way.” The success of that marketing spend remains to be seen, but it can’t hurt to highlight Mr. Hershey’s ostensible purity at a time when the company that bears his name has been under fire for diluting its products with compound coatings in order to save money. And so we have a punishingly straightforward film that paints the Pennsylvania icon as a square-jawed, sweet-toothed wife guy who loved candy, orphans, and sitting way too close to the edge of the massive water tower that overlooks the town he remade in his own image.

Directed by Mark Waters, but absent any trace of the poppy confidence he once brought to the likes of “Mean Girls” and “Freaky Friday,” “Hershey” opens with its first and only stylistic flourish as a match cut transforms an immaculate chocolate Kiss into a small lump of coal — Milton Hershey’s life would turn out to be sweet, but it sure didn’t start that way. The film that follows sadly feels less like “Lawrence of Arabia” than it does an AI-generated adaptation of Hershey’s Wikipedia page, its algorithmic sense of human interaction rendered all the more uncanny by its ecclesiastical approach to conflict (and also by its blown out cinematography, which suggests a very literal interpretation of Angel Studios’ promise to produce “movies and shows that amplify light.”)

Adhering to the prosaic structure and candied morality that the Erwin brothers have made endemic to the world of faith-based biopics and their immediate kin, the film sees Hershey’s life as a blessed march towards his eternal reward — one that’s only slowed down by the litany of speed bumps that pop up along his path to heaven.

Young Milton’s very serious Mennonite mom is a major bummer, but she lets him out of the house to work for a local printer. The JRPG-like town where he grows up in the 1860s seems inhospitable to dreams, but its muddy roads make it appear as though the streets are paved with chocolate. His dad (Alan Ruck, a long way from “Succession”) abandons him pretty fast, but not before bending down to the kid like Zooey Deschanel in “Almost Famous” and telling him: “You’re a Hershey, and that means when you follow your dream, you don’t let anyone get in your way.” Apparently his dad’s dream was to not live with his family anymore, but so be it. A good example is a good example.

Every stumbling block is immediately followed by a burst of divine providence, as Sharon Paul and Timothy Michael Hayes’ script adheres to the grindset mindset of the prosperity gospel while Rolfe Kent’s saccharine score blends everything together into a tasteless slurry of unrefined sugar. The film insists that a little sweetness goes a long way, as an orgasmic taste of rock candy is all that Milton needs to make it through the day, but it doesn’t heed its own advice. Milton’s passion leads him to a job working for a saintly confectioner named Joseph Royer (a beneficent Richard Kind, as close to a live-action Bing Bong as he’s ever been), who just smiles it off when the kid forgets to turn off the peanut roaster and nearly burns down the whole shop.

Later, after sprouting into Finn Wittrock and starting his own caramel company, Milton is miraculously spared from ruin several times over by virtue of his non-denominational faith in himself and the universe. One low moment is redeemed by a massive order from overseas. Another resolves with a traveling salesman busting into the Lancaster Caramel Company with an offer to invest in chocolate — the future of snacking! “This chocolate,” Milton sniffs, “it could be good if it wasn’t so bad.” I know the feeling. The next time disaster strikes, he inadvertently stumbles upon the Hershey Kiss in the very next scene. The plotting is schematic enough to make “Bohemian Rhapsody” seem like “Last Days” by comparison.

Somewhere in there Milton enjoys a meet-cute with a woman named Kitty Sweeney (Alexandria Daddario), a grinning beauty who credits caramels with curing her shyness. Her job as Milton’s wife is to be his biggest cheerleader, and then — as the years melt away — to collapse in undiagnosed pain whenever he leaves the room. At one point it is implied that she and Milton have sexual intercourse, but only so the movie can leverage the couple’s inability to conceive a child into a robust philanthropic regime that allowed them to house and educate any number of white male orphans.

Of course, expecting this movie to acknowledge the Milton Hershey School’s history of racial and social discrimination would be as delusional as thinking its third act might address the labor disputes that unsettled Hershey’s chocolate factory in the late 1930s. Such things are simply not sweet enough to befit a story about how some vague belief and a little stick-it-to-em are all a man needs to prosper in this great land — even if a warts-and-all version of that same story would still be a model of American success.

Considerably less textured than the chocolate bars that have become synonymous with its title character, Waters’ film is so determined to launder one man’s dreams into reality that it comes to assume its own kind of dream logic in return — one divorced from the basic relationship between cause-and-effect or an event and its meaning.

In what might be the single most deranged movie scene of the year, Milton and his ailing wife Kitty literally dance for joy on the bow of a ship after learning that a twist of fate has spared them from being aboard the Titanic, even though upwards of 1,400 other people went to a watery grave that night. I’m not sure that qualifies as bringing the brand’s “story into the culture in a more immersive way,” but it’s definitely what I’m going to be thinking about the next time I bite into a milky and delicious Hershey Bar. After watching this perversely chalky film about the company’s founder, it’s a wonder that I can still remember what their signature product even tastes like.

Angel Studios will release “Hershey” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

#3417. These Like-New Kindles Are up to $75 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. All five are a generation behind Amazon's current lineup: The company introduced redesigned Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (plus accessories) in October, with the new Paperwhite now starting at $199.99, and replaced the 2024 Scribe with a third-generation model in December 2025. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. As PCMag notes in its review, it's a great option for readers who don't need color or handwriting features.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $190.99 from $224.99, making it just $38 more than the like-new Paperwhite (16GB). For that relatively small difference, you're doubling the storage to 32GB and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is down to $220.99 from $260.99 and offers something the Paperwhite models can’t: a color E-Ink display, which makes it well suited to comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, and travel guides. Its seven-inch screen shows that color content at 150ppi while keeping text at a sharp 300ppi, and you can mark passages in multiple highlight colors to keep your notes organized. That said, colors are noticeably more muted than on a conventional tablet, and battery life tops out at eight weeks, compared with 12 weeks on the Paperwhite.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $243.99 from $287.99, making it just $23 more than the standard like-new Colorsoft. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3415. Apple TV’s Masterpiece Spy Thriller Series Is So Good, It’s Renewed For 4 More Seasons

Apple TV's spy thriller series has scored an unprecedented win on streaming, with four more seasons confirmed to be on the way, and it just proves how the show is unmatched when it comes to the genre. The espionage genre has become the talk of the town lately, as all eyes turned to one of the biggest movie franchises of all time.

After all, Dune director Denis Villeneuve was charged with casting Daniel Craig's replacement as James Bond for the suave spy's new movie. After a long casting process with many rumors and conflicting reports, The Batman star Robert Pattinson has been officially announced to play James Bond. That reveal comes on the same day that one of Apple TV's best shows released its own exciting future update.

In a competitive streaming market where espionage thrillers have become some of the most popular shows around, Apple TV continues to thrive with a long-running British spy series. The show in question faces competition from hits like Michael Fassbender's The Agency, Gabriel Basso's The Night Agent, Richard Madden's Citadel, John Krasinski's Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan, and more genre successes.

However, only Slow Horses has managed to go the distance with six seasons so far, and all of them being released on an annual schedule. In fact, the first two seasons of Slow Horses arrived on Apple TV in the same year, 2022, showing how the spy thriller differs from its genre competition. Now, Slow Horses just got a massive future update that further sets it apart from other espionage TV shows.

The Slow Horses season 6 finale aired on October 21, but the show's future was already confirmed to extend well beyond its latest season. After all, Apple TV renewed Slow Horses for season 7 in July 2025, while the hit show was confirmed to come back for season 8 more recently, in September, right before Slow Horses season 6 was released on the streaming service. Based on the Mick Herron series of novels following the agents of Slough House, seasons 7 and 8 will be based on the books Bad Actors and Clown Town, respectively, but that is not all.

Slow Horses boasts a near-perfect 97% overall critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes for its six seasons.

Recently, Sid Baker actress Olivia Cooke, who returned to the show in season 6 after a prolonged absence, indicated that Slow Horses might call it a day after season 8. Talking to The Times, Cooke claimed she was shooting the final season of the Apple TV spy thriller series and that the show coming to an end was "what we’ve been told." However, the future could not be brighter for fans of the espionage drama, as Apple TV has officially confirmed that Slow Horses has been renewed for seasons 9 and 10. That said, it means a major change is happening.

So far, all seasons of Slow Horses have had source material to adapt, mostly covering a single book of Herron's fan-favorite series of novels. However, that franchise runs out of books to adapt with the upcoming release of season 8, which should happen in 2028, if the show keeps to its annual release schedule. While Herron has plans to write more books in the franchise, he has a tighter deadline now in place if they are to be adapted, with seasons 9 and 10 likely to begin filming soon, given how Slow Horses season 8 filming is underway two years before its release.

Besides running out of source material to adapt, Slow Horses seasons 9 and 10 could have had to deal with another major change, as the presence of Jack Lowden's River Cartwright was uncertain when the series' renewal was announced. After all, the actor was a finalist for the role of the next James Bond, and if he got the role, that likely meant Slow Horses losing River, a key part of the show throughout all seasons. However, with Robert Pattinson as the new 007, Lowden is expected to remain as Slow Horses works through its four upcoming seasons.

#3413. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3412. iPhone Duo one week later: The future, or not for me?

My iPhone Duo arrived last Thursday, so I’ve had a week to use it as my daily carry. My early experience has been mixed, so I keep asking myself an important question: is this the iPhone’s future and I just need to adapt, or is the Duo simply not for everyone?

After a week using the iPhone Duo, in some ways I have a lot of clarity about the product, and in other ways my thinking is very clouded.

To put it simply: I’m not having a great time with the Duo, which makes me wonder if the problem is me, not it.

I’ve seen countless social media posts from Duo owners proclaiming how much they love the product. And I absolutely believe them. The iPhone Duo is a remarkable innovation for the iPhone. It’s cool, weird, and wonderful in all sorts of ways. But for me and my needs (preferences?), it’s been more frustrating than enjoyable.

And that frustration mainly boils down to one thing: I almost never want to open it.

I’d estimate at least 90% of my iPhone Duo usage involves the front display. And when I unfold it the remaining 10% of the time, it’s often because I force myself to do it in the hopes of discovering what I’m missing out on. Like, I know I should be unfolding it more, so I do. But it doesn’t add any real value for me.

Because I rarely want to open the iPhone Duo, I’m left using the outer display all the time. In that mode, the Duo is too heavy for extended use, too wide to comfortably reach, and the UI in most apps is an adjustment.

Are these dealbreakers? No. I could live with the Duo’s outer display if I had to, but it’s definitely an inferior experience to my iPhone 18 Pro.

If I was opening the iPhone Duo more, and actually taking advantage of the key value proposition of foldables—that you can unfold them—I doubt the outer screen would bother me much.

But what I’ve found, at least so far, is that one-handed iPhone use is very important to me, which rules out using the inner display. I use my iPhone mostly for quick interactions, and often with a child in one hand (I have three very young kids). In situations when I do have two hands free to open the Duo, I’m probably sitting in front of my iPad Pro with a Magic Keyboard attached and would rather use the iPad instead.

So again: is the problem with the Duo, or with me?

I think foldables and slab phones will obviously coexist as there will be fans of each.

I’m absolutely already converted however and am loving my duo.

Considering the Air was my favourite phone up until this it’s surprised me. I love proper one handed use again on the outside screen and unfolded it’s much nicer than my old mini 7.

I get it’s not for everyone but those that click with it like myself have a superb device!

I think it’s the latter, but I’m not sure “problem” is the right word. I just don’t find myself using it the way it’s meant to be used. And that’s fine.

I want to love the iPhone Duo, because I see how much fun other people are having with it. And maybe given more time, something will click and I’ll start to use it “as intended.”

If iPhone Duo is the future of the iPhone, I’ll adapt and move on with my life. But one week in, I think it’s probably just not for me. And if it’s not for me, maybe there are a lot of people who will continue preferring non-foldable iPhones for many years to come.

What’s your iPhone Duo experience been like? Are you loving it or struggling? Let us know in the comments.

#3411. 54 Years Ago, Peanuts Went From Meh To Masterpiece With Just One Comic

Volumes have been written about what makes Peanuts great. And rightly so. But what about the moment when Peanuts became great? That's a different story. What was the comic where things really clicked for Charles M. Schulz? Where Peanuts leveled up and officially became what it was destined to be? It all goes back to a small but significant milestone for the strip's unexpected breakout hit character: Snoopy.

The Peanuts Gang never grew up. They might have celebrated birthdays now and then, but they never got older. They never matured. They did, however, evolve, especially early in the strip's 50-year run. And no character evolved faster, or more significantly, than Snoopy. The black-and-white beagle started out as a canine companion, a scrappy sidekick for Charlie Brown. By 2000, when Peanuts ended, Snoopy was the star of the show, and arguably had the most developed personality out of the whole Gang.

Over time, Snoopy's internal monologue became a Peanuts staple. It became familiar to readers to watch him react in his head, via thought balloon, to something Charlie Brown, or Lucy, or Linus just said. Or to carry on entire, one-sided conversations with himself. Or to lapse into fantasy entirely, imagining himself as a World War I pilot or a famous writer. Snoopy's interior life became more fleshed out than many of Peanuts' more ancillary characters.

To get to that point, there had to be a first time Snoopy had a thought. Or otherwise, the first time the audience was privy to what Snoopy was thinking. It might have just been a fun wrinkle for Charles Schulz to throw into the mix at the time, but it wound up having a profound effect on Peanuts, helping seal its place in pop culture in perpetuity.

It is May 1952. Peanuts has been running for about a year and a half. It is still trying to get its syndication numbers up to 50 newspapers across the United States. The strip has steady momentum. Back in January, it started running extra-sized Sunday strips, a signal that publisher United Features Syndicate and the editors at the papers that bought Peanuts believed in it.

It is a milestone year creatively too. Lucy van Pelt debuts in March. Linus, her brother, first appears later that fall. The catchphrase "good grief" pops up for the first time. The infamous "football gag" starts before the end of the year. And Snoopy, most of all, becomes a main cast member. That starts in May, when his interiority is depicted for the first time.

Originally, Snoopy looked quite different from the droopy-eared, peanut-headed icon he's known as today, starring in a beautifully minimalistic strip.

Before considering the moment everything changed for Snoopy, it is worth putting his look under the microscope. In '52, the beagle is still barely more than a doodle of a dog. He hasn't taken on his more recognizable form yet. That's still a few years off. So, to get all philosophical for a moment, like Peanuts was occasionally prone to, existence preceded essence for Snoopy, but once he gained the essential component of an interior monologue, he was finally able to evolve into the beloved pop culture icon that has existed ever since.

May 27, 1952. It is a Tuesday. Readers in 40-45 newspapers, from Allentown, Pennsylvania to Seattle, Washington open up the funny pages to find this strip. In the first frame, Snoopy sits serenely on the lawn, minding his own business. In the second panel, along comes Charlie Brown, humming some tune to himself. In panel three, Charlie Brown playfully tugs on Snoopy's ear and says, "kind of warm out today for ear muffs, isn't it?"

It is a dumb joke. A childish joke. Which makes sense. It is made by a child. But it is playful, and innocent enough. It is a joke, but it isn't this Peanuts strip's punchline. Instead, it is the set-up for the punchline, which comes in the final frame. For readers at the time, in '52, it would have been a delightful surprise. Snoopy can speak like a human! Or at least, think like one.

"Why do I have to suffer such indignities?" Snoopy thinks, walking away in a huff. The dog's thought bubble is a squiggly line, perhaps to convey that Snoopy is rattled by the interaction, or maybe just to visually differentiate it from the human Peanuts characters' dialogue. Either way, that stylistic touch wouldn't last, but what would is the portrayal of Snoopy as not just thinking complex human thoughts, but having complex human emotions.

Sure, Snoopy would become a bit more Zen as time went on, but he also demonstrated a temper at times. In this gamechanging Peanuts comic, he's indignant at having his idyllic moment interrupted. The foundations of Snoopy's long-term character had already been laid by the time Charles M. Schulz decided to give him an internal voice; that decision allowed Schulz to build Snoopy up from there in ways that never would have been possible otherwise.

Within a few years of Snoopy's first thought, Peanuts exploded in popularity. The strip went from appearing in dozens of newspapers to hundreds. It got media attention, as a result of its exponential growth and developing fandom. Snoopy's voice, and Snoopy's personality, were arguably the missing pieces of the puzzle that pushed Peanuts from good to great, from "meh" to masterpiece.

Another big moment for Snoopy in '52 was the first time he danced, something that would become a key part of his character when the Peanuts Gang made the jump to TV in the 1960s. It was another step toward humanizing him as a character. In turn, it was another level of depth added to Peanuts, opening up a whole new world of jokes for the series to make. So, this was a pivotal moment for more than just furthering the strip's appeal to readers. It was also critical to the longevity of Peanuts.

The Peanuts have many classic comics that are amazing, but here are seven comic strips related to Snoopy that are genuine 10/10 masterpieces.

It might not have been immediately evident as a "level up" moment for Peanuts, but in retrospect, it is the moment that Charles M. Schulz figured up the missing ingredient to his series and compensated. It was when Schulz solidified his place, and his characters' place, in the pop culture canon forever.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

Written, directed by, and starring Sylvester Stallone in his follow-up to 1979’s Rocky II, and the second sequel to the legendary Rocky, Rocky III continues the pursuits of the titular world boxing star. In the third chapter of his story, Rocky Balboa faces stiff competition from James “Clubber” Lang, a young and powerful contender rising the ranks, and turns to his old adversary, Apollo Creed, to help him train for his new fight. Talia Shire, Burt Young, Carl Weathers, and Burgess Meredith reprise their roles from the previous films, with Mr. T and Hulk Hogan appearing as new characters.

At the time of its release, Rocky III was criticized for its story, but it grew into a cult favorite and is one of the most popular and culturally significant of the Rocky films. The film is mostly remembered for Carl Weathers’ performance and the Oscar-winning theme song, “Eye of the Tiger,” which has​ since become synonymous with sports/training montages in films. Undoubtedly a flashy, high-energy blockbuster, Rocky III transformed the franchise from a grounded underdog drama into a larger-than-life 1980s pop-culture phenomenon.

Not to be confused with the 1991 live-action film, 2019’s The Addams Family is an animated adaptation of Charles Addams’ comic strip featuring the creepy and kooky titular family. The supernatural comedy film follows the Addams as they relocate to a humble suburban town in New Jersey, where their peaceful, macabre life is threatened once again when a reality TV show host tries to get rid of them. The ensemble voice cast includes Oscar Isaac, Charlize Theron, Chloë Grace Moretz, Finn Wolfhard, Snoop Dogg, and Bette Midler as the core family members.

Directed by Conrad Vernon and Greg Tiernan, The Addams Family puts a colorful spin on the deliciously dark original material, transforming Charles Addams’s demure world into a dazzling animated extravaganza. The film not only shifts the tone and style of its origin but also the storytelling, while keeping the eccentricity of the characters intact. When it was released, the film did not fare well among critics but was a box office success and earned praise for its animation style and quirky reinterpretation of the original characters.

#3408. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.
